parole.testo: From Middle English demonstratif, from Middle French démonstratif, from Latin dēmōnstrātīvus. Equivalent to demonstrate + -ive.

parole.significato: To demonstrate.
parole.testo: From Middle French demonstrer, from Old French demonstrer, demoustrer, from Latin dēmonstrō, with re-Latinized spelling.

parole.significato: To indicate; to mark.
parole.testo: From Middle French denoter, from Latin denotare, from de- (“complete”) and notare (“to mark out”).

parole.significato: Having relatively high density.
parole.testo: From Middle French dense, from Latin dēnsus, from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“thick, dense”) (whence also Ancient Greek δασύς (dasús)).

parole.significato: The amount of a certain phenomenon (such as stuff, things, energy, or otherwise) in a given area (surface area) or volu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French densité or Latin densitas. Morphologically dense + -ity.

parole.significato: The act of stripping off covering, or removing the surface; a making bare.
parole.testo: From Middle French dénudation, from Latin denudatio.

parole.significato: To divest of all covering; to make bare or naked; to strip.
parole.testo: From Middle French dénuder, from Latin dēnūdāre, from dē- + nūdus (“bare”).

parole.significato: Relying upon; depending upon.
parole.testo: From Middle English dependaunt, dependent, from Middle French dependant (present participle of dependre (“to depend”)) and Latin dēpendēns (present participle of dēpendeō (“to depend”)). By surface analysis, depend + -ent.

parole.significato: To bewail; to weep bitterly over; to feel sorrow for.
parole.testo: From Middle French déplorer, from Old French deplorer, from Latin dēplōrāre (“to lament over, bewail”), from dē- + plōrāre (“to wail, weep aloud”); origin uncertain.

parole.significato: Detraction; depreciation.
parole.testo: From Middle French dépravation, from Latin dēprāvātiō (“perversion, distortion, corruption, depravity”).

parole.significato: The act of deprecating.
parole.testo: From Middle French deprecation (French: déprécation), from Latin dēprecātiōnem, from dēprecātiō (“deprecation, invocation”), from dēprecor (“to avert, warn off; to deprecate”).

parole.significato: An act of consuming agricultural resources (crops, livestock), especially as plunder.
parole.testo: From Middle French déprédation, from Latin depraedatio.

parole.significato: The act of deputing, or of appointing or commissioning a deputy or representative; office of a deputy or delegate; vice…
parole.testo: From Middle French députation, from Late Latin deputatio.

parole.significato: A leading or drawing off of water from a stream or source.
parole.testo: From Middle English derivacioun, borrowed from Middle French dérivation, from Latin dērīvātiō, dērīvātiōnem. Morphologically derive + -ation.

parole.significato: Obtained by derivation; not radical, original, or fundamental.
parole.testo: From Middle French dérivatif, from Latin dērīvātus, perfect passive participle of dērīvō (“to derive”). Related to derive; by surface analysis, derive + -ative.

parole.significato: Descending; going down.
parole.testo: From Middle English dessendaunte, borrowed from Middle French, from Latin dēscendēns, present participle of descendere, from dē + scandere (“to climb, ascend”).

parole.significato: The state or process of being desiccated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dessiccation, from Late Latin desiccatio, desiccationem, from Latin desicco.

parole.significato: To cease to proceed or act; to stop (often with from).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French desister, from Latin dēsistō, from dē- + sistō (whence de-).

parole.significato: The act of desolating or laying waste; destruction of inhabitants; depopulation.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English desolacioun, from Middle French, Old French desolacion f, from Latin dēsōlātiō f.

parole.significato: A ruler with absolute power; a tyrant.
parole.testo: From Middle French despote, from Old French despote, from Medieval Latin despota, from Ancient Greek δεσπότης (despótēs, “lord, master, owner”). Cognate with Sanskrit दम्पति (dámpati).

parole.significato: Causing destruction; damaging.
parole.testo: From Middle English destructyve, from Middle French destructif, from Latin dēstrūctīvus, from past participle of dēstruere (“to tear down, destroy”) + -īvus.

parole.significato: The state when something (for example, a custom or a law) is no longer observed nor practised; disuse, obsolescence.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English desuetude, dissuetude (“discontinuance of a practice, disuse”), from Middle French désuétude (“obsolescence”) (modern French désuétude), from Latin dēsuētūdo (“discontinuance of a practice or a habit, disuse”), from dēsuētus + -tūdō (“suffix forming abstract nouns indicating

parole.significato: The act of detaining or the state of being detained; hindrance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French détention, from Latin detentio, detentionem. Equivalent to detain + -tion.

parole.significato: To dislike (someone or something) intensely; to loathe.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Middle French detester (French détester), from Latin dētestor (“to imprecate evil while calling the gods to witness", "denounce", "hate intensely”), from dē- + testor (“to testify, bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”); see test, testify. Doublet of detestate.

parole.significato: To take away; to withdraw or remove.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French détracter, from Latin detractum, past participle of detraho.

parole.significato: The act of deviating; wandering off the correct or true path or road.
parole.testo: From Middle French deviation, from Medieval Latin deviatio. Morphologically deviate + -ion.

parole.significato: Duty, business; something that one must do.
parole.testo: From Middle English devoir, borrowed from Middle French devoir, from Old French deveir, from Latin dēbēre (“to owe; ought, must”).

parole.significato: A rolling down.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dévolution, from Medieval Latin devolutio, devolutionis, from Latin devolvo.

parole.significato: Skill in performing tasks, especially with the hands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dextérité, from Latin dexteritas, from dexter (“on the right”), this is in reference to most people having greater fine motor skills in their right hand. Partially displaced native Old English handcræft, whence Modern English handcraft.

parole.significato: Of, being, or pertaining to a devil or the Devil.
parole.testo: From Middle English diabolik, from Middle French diabolique, from Late Latin diabolicus, from Ancient Greek διαβολικός (diabolikós, “devilish”), from διάβολος (diábolos, “devil”). First attested in 1350–1400.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a deacon or the diaconate.
parole.testo: From Middle French diaconal, from Latin diaconus (“deacon”).

parole.significato: Joining two nonadjacent vertices (of a polygon or polyhedron).
parole.testo: From Middle French diagonal, from Latin diagōnālis, from Ancient Greek διαγώνιος (diagṓnios, “from angle to angle”), from διά (diá, “across”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle”).

parole.significato: A graduated, circular scale over which a needle moves to show a measurement (such as speed).
parole.testo: The original meaning was 'sundial' and/or 'clock dial'; from Middle English diall, from Middle French dyal, from Latin diālis (“daily, concerning the day”), because of its use in telling the time of day, from Latin diēs (“day”). Compare Spanish dial and día (“day”).

parole.significato: A lect (often a regional or minority language) as part of a group or family of languages, especially if they are viewed…
parole.testo: From Middle French dialecte, from Latin dialectos, dialectus, from Ancient Greek διάλεκτος (diálektos, “conversation, the language of a country or a place or a nation, the local idiom which derives from a dominant language”), from διαλέγομαι (dialégomai, “to participate in a dialogue”), from διά (di

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or measured across a diameter.
parole.testo: From Middle French dyametral, from Medieval Latin diametrālis.

parole.significato: Something transparent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French diaphane, from Medieval Latin diaphanus (“transparent”), borrowed from Ancient Greek δῐᾰφᾰνής (dĭăphănḗs), from δῐᾰφαίνω (dĭăphaínō, “to shine; to be manifest”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, dia- + -phane.

parole.significato: A gastrointestinal disorder characterized by frequent and very soft or watery bowel movements.
parole.testo: From Middle English diaria, from Middle French diarrie (French diarrhée), from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”). By surface analysis, dia- + -rrhea. Spelling later altered to resemble the word's Latin and

parole.significato: Dated spelling of diarrhoea.
parole.testo: From Middle French diarrie (French diarrhée), from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”). Spelling later altered to resemble the word's Latin and Greek roots.

parole.significato: Synonym of dictate.
parole.testo: From Middle French dictatorie, from Classical Latin dictātor + Middle French -ie. By surface analysis, dictate + -ory.

parole.significato: Office of a dictator; dictatorship.
parole.testo: From Middle English dictature, from Middle French dictature and its etymon Classical Latin dictātūra. By surface analysis, dictate + -ure.

parole.significato: To spread (something) over or through as in air, water, or other matter, especially by fluid motion or passive means.
parole.testo: From Middle French diffuser, from Latin diffūsus, past participle of diffundere, from dis- + fundere.

parole.significato: One who directs; the person in charge of managing a department or directorate (e.g., director of engineering), project,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French directeur and its source Late Latin dīrēctōrem, from Latin dīrēctus. By surface analysis, direct + -or.

parole.significato: Possible to discern; detectable or derivable by use of the senses or the intellect.
parole.testo: From Middle French discernable; spelling changed from -a- to -i- in the 17th century to conform to Latin discernibilis. By surface analysis, discern + -ible.

parole.significato: To open up; unfasten.
parole.testo: From Middle English disclosen, from Middle French desclos, from Old French desclore, itself from Vulgar Latin disclaudere, from Latin dis- + claudere (“to close, shut”) or as a variant of discludo, discludere (cf. disclude). By surface analysis, dis- + close.

parole.significato: Verbal exchange, conversation.
parole.testo: From Middle English discours, borrowed from Middle French discours (“conversation, speech”), from Latin discursus (“the act of running about”), from Latin discurrō (“run about”), from dis- (“apart”) + currō (“run”). Spelling modified by influence of Middle French cours (“course”). Doublet of discurs

parole.significato: Of or concerning discourse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French discursif, formed from the stem of Latin discursus and the suffix -if, and in part borrowed from Medieval Latin discursivus. By surface analysis, discourse + -ive.

parole.significato: To cause an intense dislike for something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French desgouster, from Old French desgouster (“to put off one's appetite”), from des- (“dis-”) + gouster, goster (“to taste”), from Latin gustus (“a tasting”). By surface analysis, dis- + gust (“taste”). The noun is from Middle French desgoust, from the verb.

parole.significato: Not connected; separated.
parole.testo: From Middle English disjunctief, disjunctyf, from Middle French disjunctif and Latin disjunctīvus (“placed in opposition”).

parole.significato: A dime minted in 1792.
parole.testo: From Middle French dixme, Old French disme (“tenth, tithe”), from Latin decimus (“tenth”). Doublet of dime.

parole.significato: Absence of order; state of not being arranged in an orderly manner.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French desordre (modern French désordre), from Old French desordre, from des- + ordre; by surface analysis, dis- + order (<< Latin ōrdō). Compare typologically Russian непоря́док (neporjádok), беспоря́док (besporjádok), неуря́дица (neurjádica) (akin to ряд (rjad), поря́док (porj

parole.significato: The state of being unequal; difference.
parole.testo: From Middle French disparité, from Latin disparitātem, accusative of disparitās, from dispār + -tās, from dis- + pār. By surface analysis, dis- + parity.

parole.significato: To scatter in different directions.
parole.testo: From Middle French disperser, from Latin dispersus, past participle of dispergō (“to scatter abroad, disperse”), from dis- (“apart”) + spargō (“to scatter”); see sparse.

parole.significato: The way in which something or someone is disposed or disposed of (in any sense of those terms); thus:
parole.testo: From Middle English disposicioun, from Middle French disposition, from Latin dispositiōnem, accusative singular of dispositiō, from dispōnō. By surface analysis, dispose + -ition. Doublet of dispositio.

parole.significato: Intending to, resulting in, or capable of disposition (disposing, disposing of, or settling a matter).
parole.testo: From Middle French dispositif and its source, Latin dispositus. Compare Piedmontese dispositiv.

parole.significato: An act of expressing dissent, especially spoken.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dissencioun, from Middle French dissention, discention, from Old French dissension, from Latin dissensio.

parole.significato: A harsh, discordant combination of sounds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dissonance, from Latin dissonantia; by surface analysis, dis- + son- + -ance.

parole.significato: To convince not to try or do.
parole.testo: From Middle French dissuader, from Latin dissuādeō (“to urge differently”, “to advise against”, “to dissuade”), from dis- (“away from”, “asunder”) + suādeō (“to recommend”, “to advise”, “to urge”).

parole.significato: Something that distracts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French distraction, from Latin distractio. Equivalent to distract + -ion.

parole.significato: Relating to distribution.
parole.testo: From Middle French distributif, from Latin distribūtīvus.

parole.significato: Synonym of diversify.
parole.testo: Hypercorrection of diversify, on the basis of Latin dīversificō + -ate (verb-forming suffix) with diversify being the regular derived form of Middle French diversifier, itself from Medieval Latin dīversificō, from Latin dīversus (“opposite, different”).

parole.significato: A cash payment of money by a company to its shareholders, usually made periodically (e.g., quarterly or annually).
parole.testo: From Middle French dividende, from Latin dīvidendum (“thing to be divided”), future passive participle of dīvidō (“to divide”), by surface analysis, divide + -end.

parole.significato: To foretell (something), especially by the use of divination.
parole.testo: Replaced Middle English devine, devin from Middle French deviner, from Latin dīvīnō.

parole.significato: Ready to accept instruction or direction; obedient; subservient.
parole.testo: From Middle English docyle, from Middle French docile, from Latin docilis, from docēre (“teach”). Compare Portuguese dócil ("docile").

parole.significato: The quality of being docile.
parole.testo: From Middle French docilité, from Latin docilitas.

parole.significato: An original or official paper used as the basis, proof, or support of anything else, including any writing, book, or ot…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French document, from Latin documentum.

parole.significato: Adhering only to principles which are true a priori, rather than truths based on evidence or deduction.
parole.testo: From Middle French dogmatique and its etymon, Late Latin dogmaticus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek δογματικός (dogmatikós, “didactic”), from δόγμα (dógma, “dogma”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the home.
parole.testo: From Middle French domestique, from Latin domesticus, from domus (“house, home”).

parole.significato: A home or residence.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English domicelle, domicylie, from Middle French domicile and directly from Latin domicilium.

parole.significato: Power or the use of power; sovereignty over something; stewardship, supremacy.
parole.testo: From Middle English dominion, from Middle French dominion, from Latin dominium (“lordship, right of ownership”), from dominus (“lord”), from domus (“house”). See demain, demesne, domain, dominium.

parole.significato: A voluntary gift or contribution for a specific cause.
parole.testo: From Middle English donacion, donation, from Middle French donation, from Latin dōnātiō (“a present”), from dōnō (“to give”), from dōnum (“a gift”). Recorded in English since the 15th century. Equivalent to donate + -ion.

parole.significato: The process of falling asleep.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dormition, from Latin dormītiōnem.

parole.significato: A measured portion of medicine taken at any one time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dose, from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, “a portion prescribed”, literally “a giving”), used by Galen and other Greek physicians to mean an amount of medicine, from δίδωμι (dídōmi, “to give”). Mostly displaced English drench. Doublet of doos.

parole.significato: Dowry.
parole.testo: From Middle English dote (“endowment”) (c. 1450), from Middle French dote (modern dot), from Latin dos.

parole.significato: To endow, donate.
parole.testo: From Middle French doter, Latin dōtāre.

parole.significato: A widow holding property or title derived from her late husband.
parole.testo: From Middle French douagere, douagiere, from douage (“dower”), from the verb douer (“to endow”), from Latin dōtō (“to endow”), from dōs (“dowry”).

parole.significato: The process of doubting or the state of being in doubt; hesitation, uncertainty.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English dubytacion, from Middle French dubitation, from Latin dubitātiō.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a duke, a duchess, or the duchy or dukedom they hold.
parole.testo: From Middle French ducal, from Latin ducālis. Doublet of dogal.

parole.significato: The act of duplicating.
parole.testo: From Middle English duplicacioun, from Middle French duplication, from Late Latin duplicātiō, duplicātiōnem, from Latin duplicō. Morphologically duplicate + -ion.

parole.significato: A series of rulers or dynasts from one family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dynastie, from Late Latin dynastia, from Ancient Greek δυναστεία (dunasteía, “power, dominion”).

parole.significato: Not at or in the centre; away from the centre.
parole.testo: From Middle French excentrique, from Medieval Latin eccentricus, from Ancient Greek ἔκκεντρος (ékkentros, “not having the earth as the center of an orbit”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + κέντρον (kéntron, “point”). Equivalent to ex- + -centric.

parole.significato: Now chiefly home economics: the art or science of household management, especially relating to the appropriate organiza…
parole.testo: From economic (noun) (obsolete) + -s (suffix forming pluralia tantum, and regular plural forms of nouns). Economic is derived from Middle English economike, iconomique (“household management”), and then: * from Middle French iconomique, oeconomique, and Old French iconomike (“(noun) household manage

parole.significato: The work involved in performing an activity; exertion.
parole.testo: From Middle French effort, from Old French esfort, deverbal of esforcier (“to force, exert”), from Vulgar Latin *exfortiō, from Latin ex + fortis (“strong”). Compare typologically Bulgarian усилие (usilie), Czech úsilí, Polish wysiłek, Russian уси́лие (usílije) (< Proto-Slavic *sila).

parole.significato: To give self-confidence to.
parole.testo: From Middle French effronter, from Old French esfronter, from Late Latin effrontō, from the prefix ex- (“from”) + frōns (“forehead”).

parole.significato: Poured out freely; profuse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French effuser, from Latin effusus, past participle of effundere (“to pour out”).

parole.significato: A liquid outpouring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French effusion, from Latin effūsiō (“outpouring”). Displaced native Old English āgotennes.

parole.significato: The act of ejecting.
parole.testo: From Middle French éjection, from Latin eiectio.

parole.significato: To pass or move by.
parole.testo: From Middle French elapser, from Latin elapsus.

parole.significato: Grace, refinement, and beauty in movement, appearance, or manners.
parole.testo: From Middle French élégance, from Latin ēlegantia (“exquisiteness; refinement, elegance”).

parole.significato: Characterised by or exhibiting elegance; having grace, refinement, or tasteful simplicity.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English elegaunt, from Middle French elegant, ultimately from Latin ēlegāns, collateral form of present participle of ēligere, from ex- (“out of, from”) + legō (“choose, select, appoint”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to an elegy.
parole.testo: From Middle French élégiaque, from Latin elegīacus, from Ancient Greek ἐλεγειακός (elegeiakós).

parole.significato: A mournful or plaintive poem; a funeral song; a poem of lamentation.
parole.testo: From Middle French elegie, from Latin elegīa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐλεγείᾱ (elegeíā), ellipsis of ἐλεγείᾱ ᾠδή (elegeíā ōidḗ, “an elegiac song”).

parole.significato: Allowed to and meeting the necessary conditions required to participate in or be chosen for something.
parole.testo: From Middle French eligible, from Latin eligibilis, from ēligō (“to select, to choose”).

parole.significato: Enamel (“an opaque, glossy coating”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French email, from Old French esmal (“enamel”) (modern French émail (“enamel; vitreous enamel; glaze (coating on pottery)”)), from Medieval Latin smaltum (“enamel”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meld- (“to melt; to soften”). Doublet of smalt, smalto, and schmaltz.

parole.significato: To come into view.
parole.testo: First attested in the late 16th century. Borrowed from Middle French emerger, from Latin ēmergō (“to rise up or out”), from ē- (a variant of ex- (“out, forth”)) + mergō (“to dip, to sink”)

parole.significato: Noteworthy, remarkable, great.
parole.testo: From Middle French éminent, from Latin present participle ēminēns, ēminentis, from verb ēmineō (“to project, protrude”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + mineō, related to mons (English mount). Compare with imminent. Unrelated to emanate, which is instead from mānō (“to flow”). Displaced native Old Engli

parole.significato: Something which is emitted or sent out; issue.
parole.testo: First attested in 1607. From Middle French émission, from Latin ēmissiō (“sending forth”), from ēmittō (“send out”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mittō (“send”).

parole.significato: Movement; agitation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French emotion (modern French émotion), from émouvoir (“excite”), based on Latin ēmōtus, past participle of ēmoveō (“to move out, move away, remove, stir up, irritate”), from ē- (“out”) (variant of ex-), and moveō (“move”).

parole.significato: The occupation or work for which one is used, and often paid.
parole.testo: From employ (itself from Middle French employer, from Middle French empleier, from Latin implicō (“enfold, involve, be connected with”), itself from in- + plicō (“fold”)) + -ment.

parole.significato: The endeavor or desire to equal or excel someone else in qualities or actions.
parole.testo: From Middle French émulation, from Latin aemulātiō.

parole.significato: A leafy salad vegetable, Cichorium endivia, which is often confused with common chicory (Cichorium intybus).
parole.testo: From Middle French endive, from Medieval Latin endivia or Italian indivia~endivia, from Byzantine Greek ἐντύβιον (entúbion), from Latin intibus (which see). The ultimate source is likely Semitic.

parole.significato: The impetus behind all motion and all activity.
parole.testo: From Middle French énergie, from Late Latin energia, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia, “activity”), from ἐνεργός (energós, “active”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). The sense in physics was coined by English polymath Thomas Young in 1802 in his lectures on Natural Philosophy.

parole.significato: To amuse (someone); to engage the attention of agreeably.
parole.testo: From Middle English entertenen, from Middle French entretenir, from Old French entretenir, from entre (“among”) + tenir (“to hold”), from Latin inter + teneō (“hold, keep”). For the noun, compare French entretien. Sense of answering a phone call in Malaysian English is influenced by Malay layan “to

parole.significato: An intensity of feeling; an excited interest or eagerness.
parole.testo: First attested from 1603, from Middle French enthousiasme, from Late Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”) + οὐσία (ousía, “essence”).

parole.significato: An extended narrative poem in elevated or dignified language, celebrating the feats of a deity, demigod (heroic epic),…
parole.testo: From Middle French épique, from Latin epicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπικός (epikós), from ἔπος (épos, “word, story”).

parole.significato: An inscription in stone.
parole.testo: From Middle French epigramme, from Latin epigramma, from Ancient Greek ἐπίγραμμα (epígramma, “inscription”).

parole.significato: A short speech, spoken directly at the audience at the end of a play
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French epilogue, from Latin epilogus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos, “a conclusion, peroration of a speech, epilogue of a play”), from ἐπιλέγω (epilégō, “to say in addition”). Eclipsed Middle English lenvoie (“epilogue”) borrowed ultimately from Old French. Equivalent to

parole.significato: A term used to characterize a person or thing.
parole.testo: From Middle French épithète, from Latin epithetum, epitheton, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον (epítheton, “epithet, adjective”), the neuter of ἐπίθετος (epíthetos, “additional”), from ἐπιτίθημι (epitíthēmi, “to add on”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “in addition”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put”) (suf. possibly related

parole.significato: The embodiment or encapsulation of a class of items.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Latin epitomē, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτομή (epitomḗ, “an abridgment, also a surface-incision”), from ἐπιτέμνω (epitémnō, “to cut upon the surface, cut short, abridge”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).

parole.significato: The fact of being equal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French equalité (modern French égalité), from Latin aequālitās, aequālitātem. Doublet of equity. By surface analysis, equal + -ity

parole.significato: Occupying a position midway between two ends or sides.
parole.testo: From Middle French équidistant, from Late Latin aequidistantem, from aequī (“equal”) + distantem (“distant”). By surface analysis, equi- + distant.

parole.significato: Equipment or supplies, especially military ones.
parole.testo: From Middle French equippage, from equipper. The "carriage" sense may be influenced by Latin equus (“horse”).

parole.significato: The result of having been worn away or eroded, as by a glacier on rock or the sea on a cliff face.
parole.testo: From Middle French erosion, from Latin ērōsiō (“eating away”), derived from ērōdō. The first known occurrence in English was in the 1541 translation by Robert Copland of Guy de Chauliac's medical text The Questyonary of Cyrurygens. Copland used erosion to describe how ulcers developed in the mouth.

parole.significato: Containing an error; inaccurate.
parole.testo: From late Middle English erroneous, from Middle French erroneux, from Latin erroneus.

parole.significato: Profound knowledge acquired from learning and scholarship.
parole.testo: First attested in the 15th Century. From Middle French érudition, from Latin eruditio (“an instructing, learning, erudition”), from erudire (“to instruct, educate, cultivate”, literally “free from rudeness”), from e (“out”) + rudis (“rude”). By surface analysis, erudite + -ion.

parole.significato: A violent ejection, such as the spurting out of lava from a volcano.
parole.testo: From Middle French éruption, from Latin eruptio.

parole.significato: A superficial structure of dead tissue, usually hardened, and commonly but not necessarily dark, adhering to underlying…
parole.testo: From Middle French eschare (now escarre) or Late Latin eschara (“scar, scab”), from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “hearth, brazier, scab”). Doublet of scar.

parole.significato: A written composition of moderate length, exploring a particular issue or subject.
parole.testo: Since late 16th century, borrowed from Middle French essay, essai (“essay”), meaning coined by Montaigne at the same time, from the same words with the earlier meanings 'experiment; assay; attempt', from Old French essay, essai, assay, assai, from Latin exagium (“weight; weighing, testing on the bal

parole.significato: The inherent nature of a thing or idea.
parole.testo: From Middle English essence, from Middle French essence, from Latin essentia (“the being or essence of a thing”), from an artificial formation of esse (“to be”), to translate Ancient Greek οὐσία (ousía, “being”), from ὤν (ṓn), present participle of εἰμί (eimí, “to be, exist”). Displaced native Old E

parole.significato: Assessment, estimation, or regard; especially; favourable estimation or regard.
parole.testo: First at end of 16th century; borrowed from Middle French estimer, borrowed from Latin aestimō. See estimate and aim, an older word, partly a doublet.

parole.significato: Morality.
parole.testo: From Middle English etik, from Middle French ethique, from Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).

parole.significato: The governor of a Jewish province under the Roman Empire.
parole.testo: From Middle French ethnarque, and its sources, New Latin ethnarcha, Koine Greek ἐθνάρχης (ethnárkhēs, “ruler of a tribe or nation, title of a Jewish official”), from Ancient Greek ἔθνος (éthnos, “nation”).

parole.significato: A strait or channel of the sea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French euripe, from Latin eurīpus, from Ancient Greek Εὔρῑπος (Eúrīpos, “Euripus”).

parole.significato: To get away from by cunning; to avoid by using dexterity, subterfuge, address, or ingenuity; to cleverly escape from.
parole.testo: From Middle French évader, from Latin ēvādō (“to pass or go over; flee”), from ē (“out of, from”) + vādō (“to go; walk”). See also wade.

parole.significato: A wandering about, excursion, trip or a roving.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French evagation, evagacion or its etymon Latin ēvagātiō, from ēvagārī (“to wander forth”). See also vagary.

parole.significato: The act of eluding or evading or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge, or interrogati…
parole.testo: From Middle French évasion, from Late Latin evasionem (accusative of evasio).

parole.significato: An occurrence; something that happens.
parole.testo: From Middle French event, from Latin ēventus (“an event, occurrence”), from ēveniō (“to happen, to fall out, to come out”), from ē (“out of, from”), short form of ex + veniō (“come”); related to venture, advent, convent, invent, convene, evene, etc.

parole.significato: The act of evicting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French éviction, from Late Latin ēvictiō, from Latin ēvincō.

parole.significato: To show or demonstrate clearly; to manifest.
parole.testo: From Middle French évincer, from Latin ēvincō (“conquer entirely, prevail over; prove exhaustively”), from ē- (short form of ex- (intensive prefix)) + vincō (“conquer”). Doublet of evict.

parole.significato: Possible to avoid; avertible.
parole.testo: From Middle French evitable (modern French évitable), from Latin ēvītābilis (“avoidable”), from ēvītō (“to avoid”) + -bilis (“-able”, able or worthy to be). The former is derived from ē- (“out”) + vītō (“to avoid, evade; to shun”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dwidʰeh₁- (“separate, set apart”)

parole.significato: To avoid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French eviter, from Latin ēvītō (“to avoid”).

parole.significato: out of
parole.testo: From Middle English, from words borrowed from Middle French; from Latin ex (“out of, from”), from Proto-Indo-European *eǵ-, *eǵs- (“out”), *eǵʰs. Cognate with Ancient Greek ἐξ (ex, “out of, from”), Transalpine Gaulish ex- (“out”), Old Irish ess- (“out”), Old Church Slavonic изъ (izŭ, “out”), Russian

parole.significato: The act of demanding with authority, and compelling to pay or yield; compulsion to give or furnish; a levying by force
parole.testo: From Middle English exaccioun, exaccion, from Middle French exaction, from Old French, from Latin exāctiō.

parole.significato: To exclude; to specify as being an exception.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French excepter, from Latin exceptus.

parole.significato: The removal of some text during editing.
parole.testo: From Middle French excision, from Latin excīsiō(n).

parole.significato: To cry out suddenly, from some strong emotion.
parole.testo: From Middle French exclamer, from Latin exclāmō, exclāmāre (“call out”), from ex- + clāmō (“to call”).

parole.significato: A loud calling or crying out, for example as in surprise, pain, grief, joy, anger, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French exclamation, from Latin exclāmātiō, from exclāmō (“to cry out”) + -tiō.

parole.significato: The process of removing or ejecting material that has no further utility, especially from the body; the act of excretin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French excrétion, or Late Latin excretio, excretionis, from Latin excerno.

parole.significato: The act of offering an excuse or apology, or the fact of being excused; an excuse, a defence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French excusation, from Latin excūsātiō, from excūsō (“to excuse”).

parole.significato: Designed or fitted for execution, or carrying into effect.
parole.testo: From Middle French executif, from Latin executivus, from Latin exsequi, from ex- ‘out’ + sequi ‘follow’.

parole.significato: Something fit to be imitated; an ideal, a worthy model or role model: a desirable example.
parole.testo: From Middle English exempler, from Middle French exemplair, and its source, Latin exemplar, from Latin exemplum (“example”).

parole.significato: Exemplary.
parole.testo: From Middle English exempler, from Middle French exemplaire, and its source, Latin exemplāris. By surface analysis, example + -ar. Doublet of exemplary.

parole.significato: To show or illustrate by example.
parole.testo: From Middle English exemplifien, from Middle French exemplifier and its etymon Medieval Latin exemplificō, from Latin exemplum (“example”).

parole.significato: Free from a duty, obligation, rule, law, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle French exempt, from Latin exemptus, past participle of eximō.

parole.significato: To expel air from the lungs through the nose or mouth by action of the diaphragm, to breathe out.
parole.testo: From Middle French exhaler, from Latin exhalare, from ex (“out”) + halare (“to breathe”).

parole.significato: The demands or requirements of a situation which often demand immediate action.
parole.testo: From Middle French exigence, from Late Latin exigentia (“urgency”) (from exigēns + -ia), from exigere (“to demand”).

parole.significato: That may be exacted; demandable; requirable.
parole.testo: From Middle French exigible, from Late Latin exigibilis, from exigō (“exact, execute”) + -ibilis.

parole.significato: The quality of being meagre or scanty.
parole.testo: From Middle French exiguite, from Late Latin exiguitas. See exiguous.

parole.significato: A person, especially a priest or priestess, who is a practitioner in exorcism to force out evil spirits or demons from…
parole.testo: From Middle French exorciste, from Latin exorcista, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκιστής (exorkistḗs).

parole.significato: Foreign, especially in an exciting way.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French exotique, from Latin exōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός (exōtikós, “foreign”, literally “from the outside”), from ἐξω- (exō-, “outside”), from ἐξ (ex, “out of”).

parole.significato: The act or state of expecting or looking forward to an event as about to happen.
parole.testo: From Middle French expectation, from Latin exspectātiō, from exspectō (“expect”). By surface analysis, expect + -ation. Displaced native Old English wēn.

parole.significato: A military journey; an enterprise against some enemy or into enemy territory.
parole.testo: From Middle French expédition, and its source, Latin expeditio.

parole.significato: An act of atonement for a sin or wrongdoing.
parole.testo: From Middle French expiation, from Latin expiātiō(n) (“satisfaction”).

parole.significato: To die.
parole.testo: From Middle English expire, from Middle French expirer, from Latin expīrō, exspīrō, from ex- (“out”) + spīrō (“breathe, be alive”).

parole.significato: Able to be explained.
parole.testo: From Middle French explicable, from Latin explicabilis, from explicō (“unfold, explain”).

parole.significato: The act of opening or unfolding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French explication and its etymon Latin explicātiō, explicātiōnem. By surface analysis, explicate + -ion.

parole.significato: The process of exploring.
parole.testo: From Middle French exploration, from Latin exploratio. Morphologically explore + -ation.

parole.significato: Synonym of explorer.
parole.testo: From Middle English exploratour (“scout or spy”), from Middle French explorateur and its etymon Latin explōrātor.

parole.significato: To seek for something or after someone.
parole.testo: From Middle French explorer, from Latin explōrāre (“to investigate, search out”), itself said to be originally a hunters' term meaning "to set up a loud cry", from ex- (“out”) + plōrāre (“to cry”), but the second element is also explained as "to make to flow" (from pluere (“to flow”)). Displaced nat

parole.significato: The action of expressing thoughts, ideas, feelings, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French expression, from Late Latin expressiō, expressiōnem (“a pressing out”). Morphologically express + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of exterminating; total destruction or eradication.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French extermination, itself a learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin exterminātiō.

parole.significato: A person affiliated with an institution in a lesser capacity, for example, as a non-resident or as a part-time affiliat…
parole.testo: From Middle French externe or its etymon Latin externus.

parole.significato: Exceeding the bounds of something; roving; hence, foreign.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English extravagaunt, from Middle French extravagant and its etymon Medieval Latin extravagans, present participle of extravagor (“to wander beyond”), from Latin extra (“beyond”) + vagor (“to wander, stray”).

parole.significato: Very cheery and peppy; extremely cheerful, energetic and enthusiastic.
parole.testo: From Middle French exubérant, from Latin exūberāns, the present active participle of exūberō (“be abundant”). Put together from ex (“out”), and uber (“udder”), and originally would have referred to a cow or she-goat which was making so much milk that it naturally dripped or sprayed from the udder.

parole.significato: To rejoice; to be very happy, especially in triumph; to triumph (over).
parole.testo: From Middle French exulter, from Latin exsultō, frequentative of exsiliō (“jump up”), from ex- + saliō (“jump, leap”).

parole.significato: The act of fabricating, framing, or constructing; construction; manufacture
parole.testo: From Middle French fabrication, from Latin fabricatio. Equivalent to fabricate + -ion.

parole.significato: Easy; contemptibly easy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French facile, from Latin facilis (“easy to do, easy, doable”), from Latin facere (“to do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put”) Compare Spanish and Portuguese fácil (“easy”), Catalan fàcil, Romanian facil. First use appears c. 1484 in a translation by William

parole.significato: A group of people, especially within a political organization, which expresses a shared belief or opinion different fro…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French faction, from Latin factiō (“a group of people acting together, a political faction”), noun of process from perfect passive participle factus, from faciō (“do, make”). Doublet of fashion.

parole.significato: Something that is false; an untrue assertion.
parole.testo: Corresponding to false + -ity. From Middle French fausseté, Old French falseté, from Late Latin falsitas, from Latin falsus.

parole.significato: The state of being extremely friendly; intimacy.
parole.testo: From Middle French familiarité, from Latin familiāritātem. Displaced native Old English hīwcūþnes. Morphologically familiar + -ity.

parole.significato: Extreme shortage of food in a region.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French famine, itself from the root of Latin fames.

parole.significato: Wonderful; marvelous; excellent; extraordinarily good or great (used especially as an intensifier).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French fantastique, borrowed from Late Latin phantasticus, borrowed from Ancient Greek φᾰντᾰστῐκός (phăntăstĭkós, “imaginary, fantastic; fictional”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to shine”). Equivalent to fantasy + -tic. Doublet of fantastique.

parole.significato: A person who maintains the health and balance of horses' feet through the trimming of the hoofs and fitting of horsesho…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ferrier, from Old French ferrier, from Latin ferrārius, from ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: Proceeding from, or appointed by, fate or destiny.
parole.testo: From Middle French fatal, from Latin fātālis (“fatal”).

parole.significato: A fairy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English faie, fei (“a place or person possessed with magical properties”), from Middle French feie, fée (“fairy", "fae”), from Old French fae, from Medieval Latin fāda. More at fairy.

parole.significato: Of or relating to feces.
parole.testo: From Middle French fecal, from Latin faex, equivalent to feces + -al.

parole.significato: Dirty with faeces or other impurities
parole.testo: From Middle French feculent, from Latin faeculentus, from faex.

parole.significato: Highly fertile; able to produce offspring.
parole.testo: From Middle French fécond, from Latin fēcundus (“fertile”), which is related to fētus and fēmina (“woman”).

parole.significato: To react, using fermentation; especially to produce alcohol by aging or by allowing yeast to act on sugars; to brew.
parole.testo: From Middle English ferment, from Middle French ferment, from Latin fermentāre (“to leaven, ferment”), from fermentum (“substance causing fermentation”), possibly from contraction of *fervimentum, from fervēre. See also fervent.

parole.significato: The condition of being ferocious.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French férocité, from Latin ferocitas, from ferox (“fierce”), from ferus (“wild, savage, fierce”).

parole.significato: Of land, etc.: capable of growing abundant crops; productive.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French fertile, from Old French fertile, from Latin fertilis (“fruitful, fertile”), from ferō (“to bear, carry”).

parole.significato: The condition, or the degree, of being fertile.
parole.testo: From Middle French fertilité, from Latin fertilitās, equivalent to fertile + -ity.

parole.significato: A ruler-shaped instrument, generally used to slap naughty children on the hand.
parole.testo: From Middle French ferule (modern French férule), from Latin ferula (“giant fennel”). Doublet of ferula.

parole.significato: festive, relating to a festival or feast
parole.testo: From Middle French festal, from Latin festum (“feast”).

parole.significato: A festival or similar celebration.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English festivite, from Middle French festivité, from Latin festīvitas, equivalent to festive + -ity.

parole.significato: The killing of a fetus or embryo; an induced abortion.
parole.testo: From fetus + -cide or fetus + -icide, from Middle French -cide, from Latin -cīda (“cutter, killer”) and its derivation -cīdium (“killing”), from -cīd (combining form of caedō (“cut, kill”)) + -a (“-er”, forming agent nouns).

parole.significato: Land held in feudal tenure.
parole.testo: From Middle English feu, from Middle French fé (“fief”), fié, fief, fieu, from Latin feodum.

parole.significato: Magical or fairylike.
parole.testo: From Middle English faie, fei (“a place or person possessed with magical properties”), from Middle French feie, fee (“fairy", "fae”), from Old French fae, from Medieval Latin fāda. More at fairy.

parole.significato: Land held of a superior, particularly on condition of homage, fealty, and personal service, especially military service.
parole.testo: From Middle French fief, from Old French fief, from Medieval Latin fevum, a variant of feudum (whence also Old French fieu, fied), from Old Frankish *fehu (“cattle, livestock”), from Proto-Germanic *fehu (“cattle, sheep”), from Proto-Indo-European *peku-, *peḱu- (“sheep”). Doublet of fee, feud, and

parole.significato: The act of giving figure or determinate form.
parole.testo: Late Middle English figuracion, from Middle French figuration, from Latin figūrō (“to form”). Equivalent to figurate + -ion.

parole.significato: A skill in the handling or manipulation of a situation.
parole.testo: From Middle English finesse (“a degree of excellence; (of metal) fineness, purity”), from Middle French finesse, Old French finesse (“a fineness; a delicacy; slenderness”), from fine, fin (“fine, thin”) (from Latin fīnis (“an end”); compare Middle English fīn (“of superior quality; precious, valuabl

parole.significato: The public treasury of Rome.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle French fisc and partly from its etymon, Latin fiscus (“basket, money-bag, public treasury”); see fiscal.

parole.significato: Related to the treasury of a country, company, region or city, particularly to government spending and revenue.
parole.testo: From Middle French fiscal, from Latin fiscus (“treasury”) – see fiscus and fisc.

parole.significato: A large vessel resembling a jug, usually with a handle, lid, and spout, for serving drinks such as cider or wine at a t…
parole.testo: From Middle English flagon, flakon [and other forms], from Middle French flacon, Old French flacon, flascon (“flask”) (modern French flacon (“vial”)), from Medieval Latin flascōnem, the accusative singular of Late Latin flascō (“bottle; glass or earthenware vessel for wine; portable barrel”), from F

parole.significato: Obvious and offensive; blatant; scandalous.
parole.testo: From Middle French flagrant, from Latin flagrantem, present participle of flagrare (“blaze, burn”). More at black.

parole.significato: Capable of being flexed or bent without breaking; able to be turned or twisted without breaking.
parole.testo: From Middle French flexible, from Latin flexibilis, from flectō (“to bend, curve”). Morphologically flex + -ible.

parole.significato: The derivative of a function.
parole.testo: From Middle French fluxion, from Late Latin fluxiō, from Latin flūxus + -iō.

parole.significato: The leaves of plants.
parole.testo: From earlier foilage, from Late Middle English ffoylage, from Middle French feuillage. The more recent form is influenced by Latin folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: The act of fortifying; the art or science of fortifying places to strengthen defence against an enemy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French fortification, from Late Latin fortificatio, fortificationem, from fortifico, from Latin fortis. By surface analysis, fort + -ification.

parole.significato: Fortuitous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French fortuit, from Latin fortuitus.

parole.significato: The iron worker in charge of the blast furnace and the smelting operation.
parole.testo: From Middle French fondeur, from Latin fundo (“pour, melt, cast”).

parole.significato: A severe laminitis of a horse, caused by untreated internal inflammation in the hooves.
parole.testo: From Middle French fondrer (“send to the bottom”), from Latin fundus (“bottom”).

parole.significato: A female founder (“one who founds or casts metals”).
parole.testo: From founder (“one who founds or casts metals”) + -ess (suffix forming female forms of words). Founder is derived from Middle French fondeur (“owner of a foundry; ironworker in charge of smelting, founder”) (modern French fondeur), from Latin fundātor (“founder”) (rare): see further at etymology 1.

parole.significato: Easily broken, not sturdy; of delicate material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French fragile, from Latin fragilis, formed on frag-, the root of frangere (“to break”). Cognate with fraction, fracture and doublet of frail.

parole.significato: The condition or quality of being fragile; brittleness; frangibility.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French fragilité, from Latin fragilitās. Doublet of frailty. Morphologically fragile + -ity.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a brother or brothers.
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰréh₂tēr Borrowed from Middle French fraternel, from Medieval Latin frāternālis (“fraternal”), from Latin frāternus (“of or pertaining to a brother, fraternal”), from frāter (“brother”).

parole.significato: The killing of one's brother (or sister).
parole.testo: From Middle French fratricide or its etymon Latin frātricīdium.

parole.significato: A person who commits fratricide.
parole.testo: From Middle English fratricide, from Middle French fratricide or its etymon Latin frātricīda.

parole.significato: To shiver or shudder.
parole.testo: From Middle English fremyssh, *fremysshen, from (the stem of) Middle French fremir, from Late Latin *fremīre, from Latin fremere.

parole.significato: The rubbing of one object or surface against another.
parole.testo: From Middle French friction and directly from Latin frictionem, nom. frictio (“a rubbing, rubbing down”).

parole.significato: The state of being frigid; coldness; lack of heat.
parole.testo: From Middle English frigiditee, frigidite, a borrowing from Middle French frigidité, itself a borrowing from Latin frīgiditātem, accusative of Latin frīgiditās.

parole.significato: Synonym of pancake, a portion of batter fried on a pan.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English fryture, from Middle French friture, from Old French friture, from Vulgar Latin *frīctūra, from Latin frīgō (“to fry”); compare fry. For the development of Middle English /iu̯r(ə)/ into /ə(ɹ)/, compare armour, batter, border, solder.

parole.significato: Careful or wise in expenditure; avoiding waste.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Latin frugalis (“virtuous, thrifty”). Displaced native Old English spærhende (literally “spare-handed”).

parole.significato: The act of fulminating or exploding; detonation.
parole.testo: From Middle French fulmination, from Latin fulminātiō; equivalent to fulmine + -ation.

parole.significato: What something does or is used for.
parole.testo: From Middle French function, from Old French fonction, from Latin functiō (“performance, execution”), from functus, perfect participle of fungor (“to perform, execute, discharge”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg- (“to enjoy”).

parole.significato: A ceremony to honor and remember a deceased person, often distinguished from a memorial service by the presence of the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French funerailles pl (“funeral rites”), from Medieval Latin fūnerālia (“funeral rites”), originally neuter plural of Late Latin fūnerālis (“having to do with a funeral”), from Latin fūnus (“funeral, death, corpse”), origin unknown, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *d

parole.significato: Of or relating to a funeral.
parole.testo: From Middle French funerail, from Latin funereus + -al.

parole.significato: furiousness; fury
parole.testo: From Middle English furiosite, from Middle French furiosité or its etymon Late Latin furiōsitās, from Latin furiōsus + -itās.

parole.significato: A general uproar or commotion.
parole.testo: From Middle English furour, from Middle French fureur, from Old French furor, from Latin furor, from furō (“To rage, to be out of one's mind”).

parole.significato: Of a thing: done with evasive or guilty secrecy.
parole.testo: From Middle English *furtyve (implied in furtyvely (adverb)), from Middle French furtif, furtive (“furtive, stealthy”) (modern French furtif), from Latin fūrtīvus (“clandestine, furtive, secret; concealed, hidden; stolen”), from fūrtum (“theft; robbery”) (from fūr (“thief”), ultimately from Proto-In

parole.significato: A light flintlock musket or firelock.
parole.testo: From Middle French fusil, ultimately from Latin focus (“hearth; fire”). Doublet of fusee.

parole.significato: The act of merging separate things, or the result thereof.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1555, in a translation by Richard Eden. From Middle French fusion, from Latin fūsiōnem (the accusative of fūsiō), from fusus, past participle of fundō (“to pour; to melt”) (see also found). Doublet of foison.

parole.significato: Incapable of producing results, useless; doomed not to be successful; not worth attempting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French futile, from Latin fūtilis.

parole.significato: Any rent, charge, tribute, custom, tax, duty, excise etc.
parole.testo: A form of gavel (“rent, tax”) influenced by Middle French gabelle, from Late Latin gabella, gabulum, gablum; of uncertain origin. Compare gavel (“tribute”).

parole.significato: To show off.
parole.testo: From Middle English galery, gallerye, from Middle French galerie, gallerie, from Old French galerie, gallerie (“a long portico, a gallery”), from Medieval Latin galeria (“gallery”), of unknown origin. Perhaps an alteration of Latin galilea (“church porch”), probably from Latin Galilaea, Galilee, reg

parole.significato: The leg or shank, typically of an animal, especially of a lion, on a coat of arms, crest, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle French gambe (variant of jambe) from Late Latin gamba (hoof, leg, shank). Doublet of jamb, gamba, and gam.

parole.significato: To engender.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English gendren, from Middle French gendrer, from Latin generāre.

parole.significato: Very broad; pertaining or appropriate to large classes or groups as opposed to specific instances.
parole.testo: From Middle French générique, from Latin genus (“genus, kind”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Noble in behaviour or actions; principled, not petty; kind, magnanimous.
parole.testo: From Middle French genereux, and its source, Latin generōsus (“of noble birth”), from genus (“race, stock”).

parole.significato: Friendly and cheerful; enlivening.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French génial, borrowed from Latin geniālis (“of or pertaining to marriage; festive”), from genius (“guardian spirit”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: The study of the physical properties of the earth, including how humans affect and are affected by them.
parole.testo: From Middle French géographie, from Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía, “a description of the earth”), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + γράφω (gráphō, “write”). Doublet of geographia. Use in reference to lavatories derives from the mid-20th century euphemism "show one the geography of

parole.significato: The small mass of cells from which a new organism develops; a seed, bud, spore, or zygote.
parole.testo: From Middle French germe, from Latin germen (“bud, seed, embryo”). Doublet of germen.

parole.significato: Any spherical (or nearly spherical) object.
parole.testo: From late Middle English globe, from Middle French globe, from Old French globe, borrowed from Latin globus. Doublet of globus.

parole.significato: The act of glorifying or the state of being glorified.
parole.testo: From Middle English glorificacion, glorificacioun, from Middle French glorification and its etymon Latin glōrificātiō. By surface analysis, glorify + -ication.

parole.significato: Fibrin (formerly considered as one of the "animal humours").
parole.testo: From Middle French gluten, borrowed from Latin glūten (“glue”).

parole.significato: That which steers a nautical vessel; a rudder or a person employing it.
parole.testo: From Middle English governail, governaile from Middle French and Old French governail, from Latin gubernāculum. Doublet of gubernaculum.

parole.significato: Lean, slender, thin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French gracil, gracile (“slender, thin”) (modern French gracile (“gracile”)), or directly from its etymon Latin gracilis (“slender, slim, thin; lean, meagre, scanty; simple, unadorned”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kerḱ- (“to become thin; to wane”). The sense “graceful

parole.significato: graciousness, usually in a bad sense, as implying duplicity
parole.testo: From Middle English graciousete, partly from Middle French gracieuseté, partly modelled on Latin grātiōsitās, and probably also partly equivalent to gracious + -osity.

parole.significato: A rating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French grade (“a grade, degree”), from Latin gradus (“a step, pace, degree”), from Proto-Italic *graðus, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰradʰ-, *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”). Doublet of gradus. Cognate with Gothic 𐌲𐍂𐌹𐌸𐍃 (griþs, “step, grade”), Bavarian Gritt (“step, stride”), Lithuanian

parole.significato: Not breaching any constraints of the grammar, or morpho-syntax, of the relevant language.
parole.testo: From Middle French grammatical, from Latin grammaticālis.

parole.significato: The state of being grand or splendid; magnificence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French grandeur, from Old French grandur, from grant (French grand), from Latin grandis (“grown up, great”).

parole.significato: Lofty, pompous or bombastic speech or writing.
parole.testo: From Middle French grandiloquence, from Latin grandiloquentia, from grandiloquus, 1580s.

parole.significato: Given to using language in a showy way by using an excessive number of difficult words to impress others; bombastic; tu…
parole.testo: From Middle French grandiloquent, from Latin grandiloquus, from grandis (“great, full”) + loquēns, present participle of loquor (“to speak”). Compare eloquent.

parole.significato: Characterised by a dignified sense of seriousness.
parole.testo: From Middle French grave, a learned borrowing from Latin gravis (“heavy, important”). Compare Old French greve (“terrible, dreadful”). Doublet of grief.

parole.significato: A word or idiom of the Greek language used in another language, especially for literary effect.
parole.testo: From Middle French grecisme (modern French grécisme), from Medieval Latin graecismus, from Classical Latin graecus + -ismus. Compare Middle English Gryscysme (“Graecismus by Eberhard of Béthune”). Doublet of graecismus.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or connected to the throat.
parole.testo: From Middle French guttural, from New Latin gutturālis, from Latin guttur (“throat”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: Safe and comfortable, where humans, or other animals, can live; fit for habitation.
parole.testo: From Middle English abitable, habytable, from Middle French habitable, from Latin habitābilis (“habitable”), from habitō (“dwell, live”). By surface analysis, habit (“inhabit”) + able.

parole.significato: A dwelling or habitation.
parole.testo: From Middle English habitacle, from Middle French habitacle, from Latin habitāculum (“dwelling place”). See binnacle, habit (verb), inhabit.

parole.significato: The essential character of one's being or existence; native or normal constitution; mental or moral constitution; bodil…
parole.testo: From Middle English habitude, from Middle French habitude, from Latin habitūdō (“condition, plight, habit, appearance”), from habeō (“to have, hold, keep”).

parole.significato: A mythological creature generally depicted as a bird-of-prey with the head of a maiden, a face pale with hunger and lon…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Middle French harpie, from Latin harpyia, from Ancient Greek ἅρπυιᾰ (hárpuiă, literally “snatcher”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch, seize”). Compare rapacious. Middle English had arpie.

parole.significato: A characteristic trait of the Hebrew language. By extension it is sometimes applied to the Jewish people or their faith…
parole.testo: From Middle French hebraisme or Latin Hebraismus; equivalent to Hebra- + -ism.

parole.significato: An iron ore, mainly peroxide of iron, Fe₂O₃: iron(III) oxide.
parole.testo: From Middle French hematite, from Latin (lapis) haematites, from Ancient Greek αἱματίτης (haimatítēs) λίθος (líthos, “blood-red stone”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”). By surface analysis, hemat- + -ite.

parole.significato: Hereditary transmission of the physical and genetic qualities of parents to their offspring; the biological law by whic…
parole.testo: From Middle French heredité, from Latin hērēditas (“condition of being an heir”), from hēres (“heir”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to heresy or heretics.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French eretical and from Medieval Latin haereticālis, from haereticus, equivalent to heretic + -al. See heretic.

parole.significato: Synonym of inherit.
parole.testo: From Middle English heriten, from Middle French heriter (modern French hériter), from Old French eriter, heriter, earlier *hereter, from Latin hērēditō.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a hero or heroine; supremely noble.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle French heroïque and partly from Latin hērōicus. By surface analysis, hero + -ic.

parole.significato: An element (individual sign or glyph) of a hieroglyphic writing system.
parole.testo: First attested around 1598, a back-formation from hieroglyphic (1580s), from Middle French hiéroglyphique, from Late Latin hieroglyphicus, from Ancient Greek ἱερογλυφικός (hierogluphikós) (Plutarch τά ἱερογλυφικά [γράμματα] "hieroglyphic [writing]), ἱερόγλυφος (hierógluphos, “carver of hieroglyphs”)

parole.significato: Synonym of historical or historic.
parole.testo: From Middle English historial, from Middle French historial (French historial) and its etymon Latin historiālis. By surface analysis, history + -al. Piecewise doublet of storial.

parole.significato: Any Old World bird of genus Upupa, especially Upupa epops (Eurasian hoopoe), known for its distinctive plumage, fanlike…
parole.testo: Alteration of obsolete hoopoop, from earlier hoop, from Middle French and Old French huppe, from Latin upupa, ultimately onomatopoeic; Compare Ancient Greek ἔποψ (épops), Persian پوپو (popo).

parole.significato: The visible horizontal line (in all directions) where the sky appears to meet the earth in the distance.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English orisonte, orisoun, from Middle French horizon, horizonte, from Old French orisonte, orison, via Latin horizōn, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).

parole.significato: Perpendicular to the vertical; parallel to the plane of the horizon; level, flat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French horizontal, from horizon, horizonte, from Latin horizōn (stem horizont-).

parole.significato: The position of the planets and stars at the moment of someone's birth; a diagram of such positions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French horoscope, from Medieval Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos), from ὥρα (hṓra, “any limited time”) + σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”). By surface analysis, horo- + -scope.

parole.significato: Giving exhortation or advice; encouraging.
parole.testo: From Middle French hortatoire, from Latin hortor (“encourage”).

parole.significato: cordial and generous towards guests
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French hospitable, formed from the root of Latin hospitare with the suffix -able. Displaced native Old English cumlīþe (literally “guest-gentle”).

parole.significato: the consecrated bread or wafer of the Eucharist, host.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French hostie, from Latin hostia.

parole.significato: Not friendly; appropriate to an enemy; showing the disposition of an enemy; showing ill will and malevolence or a desir…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French hostile, from Latin hostīlis, from hostis (“enemy”). Displaced Old English fēondlīċ.

parole.significato: A worker employed at an inn, hostelry, or stable to look after horses.
parole.testo: From Middle English hostiler, from Middle French hostiler, from Old French hostelier, from Medieval Latin hostilārius, hospitālārius, from hospitāle "inn", from hospitālis "hospitable", from hospes "host, guest". Both hostler and its alternative form ostler originally meant simply "innkeeper", and a

parole.significato: Of or belonging to the species Homo sapiens or its closest relatives.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English humaigne, humayne, humain, from Middle French humain, from Old French humain, umain (“of or belonging to man”, adjective), from Latin hūmānus m (“of man, human”, adjective); see there for further details. Spelling human has been predominant since the early 18th century. Comp

parole.significato: The act of humiliating or humbling someone; abasement of pride; mortification.
parole.testo: From Middle French humiliation, from Late Latin humiliātiō, from humiliāre (“to humiliate”); see humiliate. Equivalent to humiliate + -ion.

parole.significato: Relating to the body fluids or humours.
parole.testo: From Middle English humerale, humorale, humoural, from Middle French humoral and Medieval Latin hūmorālis, from Latin hūmor. By surface analysis, humor + -al.

parole.significato: A membrane which completely or partially occludes the vaginal opening in human females.
parole.testo: From Middle French hymen, from Late Latin hymēn, from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”).

parole.significato: A tentative conjecture explaining an observation, phenomenon or scientific problem and that can be tested by further ob…
parole.testo: Recorded since 1596, from Middle French hypothese, from Late Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument, supposition”, literally “a placing under”), itself from ὑποτίθημι (hupotíthēmi, “to set before, suggest”), from ὑπό (hupó, “below”) + τίθημι (títhēmi,

parole.significato: Consisting of iambs (metrical feet with an unstressed–stressed pattern) or characterized by their predominance.
parole.testo: From Middle French iambique, from Late Latin ïambicus, from Ancient Greek ἰαμβικός (iambikós), from ἴαμβος (íambos) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: Sameness, identicalness; the quality or fact of (several specified things) being the same.
parole.testo: From Middle English ydemptite, from Middle French identité and its etymon Late Latin idemptitās, identitās, from idem (“the same”) + -tās (suffix forming abstract nouns) as a calque of Ancient Greek ταὐτότης (tautótēs, “sameness”).

parole.significato: A manner of speaking, a mode of expression peculiar to a language, language family, or group of people.
parole.testo: From Middle French idiome, and its source, Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “a peculiarity, property, a peculiar phraseology, idiom”), from ἰδιοῦσθαι (idioûsthai, “to make one's own, appropriate to oneself”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “one's own, pertaining to oneself, private, persona

parole.significato: One who worships idols; (historical) a pagan.
parole.testo: From Middle English ydolatrer, from Middle French idolatre, from Latin idololatra. Displaced native Old English dēofolġielda (literally “devil worshiper”).

parole.significato: Not noble; plebeian; common.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ignoble, from Latin ignōbilis, from in- (“not”) + gnōbilis, later nōbilis (“noble”).

parole.significato: Especially of a person: deserving of disgrace or dishonour; contemptible, despicable.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English ignominious (“disgraceful, shameful”), from Middle French ignominieux (modern French ignominieux), or from its etymon Latin ignōminiōsus (“disgraced; disgraceful, shameful, ignominious”), from ignōminia (“disgrace, dishonour, shame, ignominy”) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full o

parole.significato: Restricting or failing to sufficiently promote individual choice and freedom.
parole.testo: From Middle French illibéral, from Latin illiberalis, equivalent to il- + liberal.

parole.significato: The act of illuminating, or supplying with light; the state of being illuminated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French illumination, from Late Latin illūminātiō, from Latin illumino. Equivalent to illuminate + -ion.

parole.significato: Resulting from an illusion; deceptive, imaginary, unreal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French illusorie (modern French illusoire), derived from Latin illūsōrius (“mocking, ironical”).

parole.significato: The act of illustrating; the act of making clear and distinct.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French illustration, from Latin illūstrātiō, from illūstrō (“to illustrate”). By surface analysis, illustrate + -ion.

parole.significato: Synonym of illustrious.
parole.testo: From Middle French illustre (French illustre), from Latin illūstris (“bright, shining, brilliant, lustrous; clear, lucid; illustrious, distinguished, famous”), from illūstrō (“to illustrate”).

parole.significato: To illuminate (something).
parole.testo: From Middle English illustren, from Middle French illustrer (French illustrer), from Latin illūstrāre (“to illustrate”).

parole.significato: Having a lively or creative imagination.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymagynatif, from Middle French imaginatif, from Medieval Latin imāginātīvus. By surface analysis, imagine + -ative.

parole.significato: To form a mental image of something; to envision or create something in one's mind.
parole.testo: From Middle English ymagynen, from Middle French imaginer, from Latin imāginor, from imāginem, the accusative singular of imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”).

parole.significato: A person with limited mental capacity who can perform tasks and think only like a young child, in medical circles meani…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French imbécile, from Latin imbēcillus (“weak, feeble”), literally “without a staff”.

parole.significato: The quality of being imbecile; weakness; feebleness, especially of mind.
parole.testo: From Middle English inbecillite, from Middle French imbecilité, imbecillité, and its etymon Classical Latin imbēcillitās. By surface analysis, imbecile + -ity.

parole.significato: The act of imitating.
parole.testo: From Middle English imitacioun, from Middle French imitacion, from Old French imitacion, from Latin imitatio.

parole.significato: Permanent, enduring; that does not perish.
parole.testo: From Middle French inmarcessible (1482), later immarcescible (“that does not shrivel" or "that does not perish”), from Latin immarcescibilis (“unfading”).

parole.significato: Having no matter or substance; incorporeal.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English immaterial, inmateriall (“incorporeal; spiritual”), from Middle French immateriel (“not material”) (modern French immatériel), and from its etymon Medieval Latin immāteriālis (“not material”), from Latin im- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’))

parole.significato: Incurable; not able to be assisted by medicine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French immedicable and its source, Latin immedicābilis.

parole.significato: The act of immolating, or the state of being immolated.
parole.testo: From Middle English immolacion, from Middle French immolation, from Old French, from Latin immolatio.

parole.significato: Exempt; not subject to.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French immun, from Latin immūnis (“exempt from public service”), from in- (“not”) + mūnus (“service”).

parole.significato: To cloister, confine, imprison or hole up: to lock someone up or seclude oneself behind walls.
parole.testo: From Middle English enmuren and Middle French emmurer, both from Old French enmurer, from Latin immūrō, from in- + mūrus (“wall”). Modern spelling is modelled after the Latin.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being immutable; immutableness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French immutabilité, itself borrowed from Latin immūtābilitās. By surface analysis, immutable + -ity.

parole.significato: To pierce (something) with any long, pointed object.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Medieval Latin impālāre, from Latin palus, whence also pale.

parole.significato: Incapable of being touched or felt; incorporeal, intangible.
parole.testo: From Middle French impalpable, from Medieval Latin impalpabilis. See im- + palpable.

parole.significato: To give or bestow (e.g. a quality or property).
parole.testo: From Middle English imparten, borrowed from Middle French impartir, empartir, from Late Latin impartiō, impertiō, from im- (“in”) + Latin partiō (“divide”).

parole.significato: Perfect, without faults, flaws or errors
parole.testo: From Middle French impeccable, from Latin impeccabilis (“not liable to sin”), from im- (“not”) + peccare (“to err, to sin”).

parole.significato: Not penetrable.
parole.testo: From Middle English inpenetrabel, inpenetrabyle, from Middle French impenetrable or directly from its etymon, Latin impenetrābilis. By surface analysis, im- + penetrable.

parole.significato: Not perceptible, not detectable, too small in magnitude to be observed.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English imperceptible, from Middle French imperceptible and its etymon Medieval Latin imperceptibilis. By surface analysis, im- + perceptible.

parole.significato: Insolent, ill-mannered or disrespectful; Disregardful.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English impertinent, from Middle French impertinent, from Old French impertinent, from Latin impertinēns; by surface analysis, im- + pertinent.

parole.significato: To fix firmly or set securely or deeply.
parole.testo: From Middle French implanter, from Latin implantō. By surface analysis, im- + plant.

parole.significato: The act of implicating.
parole.testo: From Middle French implication, from Latin implicationem (accusative of implicatio). Equivalent to implicate + -ion.

parole.significato: Suggested indirectly, without being directly expressed; Implied.
parole.testo: From Middle French implicite, from Latin implicitus, past participle of implico (“to infold, involve, entangle”); see implicate.

parole.significato: To beg or plead for (something) earnestly or urgently; to beseech.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₁én The verb is borrowed from Middle French implorer (modern French implorer (“to beg, plead, implore”)), or directly from its etymon Latin implōrāre, the present active infinitive of implōrō (“to beseech, entreat, implore; to appeal to, pray to”), from im- (a variant of in- (intensifyin

parole.significato: The quality or condition of being important or worthy of note.
parole.testo: From Middle English importaunce, from Middle French importance, from Medieval Latin importantia. By surface analysis, import (“to be important”) + -ance.

parole.significato: To bother, irritate, trouble.
parole.testo: From Middle French importuner and its etymon Medieval Latin importūnor (“to make oneself troublesome”), from Latin importūnus (“unfit, troublesome”), originally "having no harbor".

parole.significato: To physically lay or place (something) on another thing; to deposit, to put, to set.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Late Middle English imposen (“to place, set; to impose (a duty, etc.)”), borrowed from Middle French imposer, and Old French emposer, enposer (“to impose (a duty, tax, etc.)”) (modern French imposer), from im-, em- (variants of en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’)) + poser (“to p

parole.significato: Something that is impossible.
parole.testo: From Middle French impossibilité, from Latin impossibilitās. By surface analysis, im- + possibility and impossible + -ity.

parole.significato: A tax, tariff or duty that is imposed, especially on merchandise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French impost, itself borrowed or adapted from Latin impōsitus, past participle of impōnō (“to impose”).

parole.significato: Someone who attempts to deceive by using an assumed name or identity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French imposteur, respelled in the Latin manner; ultimately from Latin impositor, agent form of Latin imponere (“to impose”).

parole.significato: The act or conduct of an impostor; deception practiced under a false or assumed character; fraud or imposition.
parole.testo: From Middle French imposture, from Late Latin impostura, Latin impostus.

parole.significato: Powerlessness; incapacity.
parole.testo: From Middle French impotence, from Latin impotentia.

parole.significato: Unsuitable to needs or circumstances; inappropriate; inapt.
parole.testo: From Middle French impropre, from Latin improprius (“not proper”), from in- + proprius (“proper”). By surface analysis, im- + proper.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being imprudent; lack of prudence, caution, discretion or circumspection.
parole.testo: From im- + prudence. From Middle French imprudence, from Latin imprudentia.

parole.significato: Not prudent; lacking prudence or discretion; indiscreet; injudicious; not paying attention to the consequences of one's…
parole.testo: From Middle French imprudent, from Latin imprūdens (“not foreseeing, ignorant”), prefix im- (“not”) + prūdens (“foreseeing, skilled, judicious”).

parole.significato: The quality of being impudent, not showing due respect.
parole.testo: From Middle French impudence, from Latin impudentia.

parole.significato: Immodesty; shamelessness.
parole.testo: From Middle French impudicité, from Latin impudicus (“shameless, immodest”) + Middle French -ité. By surface analysis, im- + pudic + -ity.

parole.significato: To assault, attack.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French impugner, from Latin impugnō, from im- + pugnō (“fight”), from pugnus (“fist”), as in English pugilism (“fighting with fists, boxing”).

parole.significato: A thrust; a push; a sudden force that impels.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French impulser, from Latin impulsus.

parole.significato: Having the power of driving or impelling; giving an impulse; moving; impellent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French impulsif, from Latin impulsivus.

parole.significato: Exemption from punishment.
parole.testo: From Middle French impunité, from Latin impunitas, from impunis (“without punishment”).

parole.significato: Not pure
parole.testo: From Middle French impur, from Latin impūrus.

parole.significato: The condition of being impure; because of contamination, pollution, adulteration or insufficient purification.
parole.testo: From impure + -ity. From Middle French impurité, from Latin impuritas.

parole.significato: The act of imputing or charging; attribution; ascription.
parole.testo: From Middle French imputation, from Latin imputatio.
