parole.testo: From Middle French obtrectacion and its source, Latin obtrectātiō (“disparagement”), from the participle stem of obtrectāre.

parole.significato: A favorable opportunity; a convenient or timely chance.
parole.testo: From Middle English occasioun, from Middle French occasion, from Old French occasiun, from Latin occāsiōnem, noun of action from perfect passive participle occāsus, from verb occidō, from prefix ob- (“down", "away”) + verb cadō (“fall”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or situated in, the occident, or west; western.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French occidental, from Latin occidentalis, equivalent to occident + -al.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or located within or near the occiput (back of the head) or the occipital bone.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Middle French occipital, from Medieval Latin occipitālis, from occiput (“the back of the head, occiput”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent of occiput + -al. Doublet of occipitalis.

parole.significato: A person who occupies an office or a position.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French occupant (present participle of occuper) or Latin occupāns, occupantis (present participle of occupō). By surface analysis, occupy + -ant.

parole.significato: An activity or task with which one occupies oneself; usually specifically the productive activity, service, trade, or c…
parole.testo: From Middle English occupacioun, borrowed from Middle French occupacion, occupation, from Latin occupātiō, occupātiōnis, from occupō (“occupy, seize”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to seize, grab”). By surface analysis, occupy + -ation.

parole.significato: To happen or take place.
parole.testo: Originally "meet (in argument)", borrowed from Middle French occurrer, from Latin occurrō (“run to meet, run against, befall, present itself”) from prefix ob- (“against”) + verb currō (“run, hurry, move”).

parole.significato: An actual instance when a situation occurs; an event or happening.
parole.testo: From Middle French occurrence, from Medieval Latin occurrentia. Morphologically occur + -ence.

parole.significato: Current, actual, occurring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French occurrent and its source, Latin occurrēns.

parole.significato: To grant (a privilege etc, by a government etc).
parole.testo: From Middle English octroy, from Middle French octroyer, from Old French otroiier, from Latin auctōrizō. Doublet of authorize.

parole.significato: A short poetical composition proper to be set to music or sung; a lyric poem; especially, now, a poem characterized by…
parole.testo: From Middle French ode, from Late Latin ōda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”). Doublet of Aoede.

parole.significato: To hurt the feelings of; to displease; to make angry; to insult.
parole.testo: From Middle French offendre, from Latin offendō (“strike, blunder, commit an offense”), from ob- (“against”) + *fendō (“strike”).

parole.significato: Causing offense; arousing a visceral reaction of disgust, anger, hatred, sadness, or indignation.
parole.testo: From Middle French offensif, from offendre + -if by analogy with défensif. Offendre is from Latin offendere (“to offend”); see offend.

parole.significato: The sense of smell; the detection of airborne molecules.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French olfaction /olefaction, from Latin olfactus, perfect passive participle of olfaciō (“to smell (transitive)”) + -tion.

parole.significato: Imposing or constituting a physical, mental, or figurative load which can be borne only with effort; burdensome.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English onerous, borrowed from Middle French onereux, from Old French onereus, a learned borrowing from Latin onerosus, from onus (“burden”) + -ōsus. Compare exonerate.

parole.significato: Effectual or important.
parole.testo: From Middle English operative, operatyfe, from Middle French operatif (modern French opératif) or its etymon Latin operātīvus. By surface analysis, operate + -ive.

parole.significato: Conjectural; expressing an opinion rather than a fact.
parole.testo: From opine + -ate + -ive. Middle French opinatif, and its source, Late Latin opinativus, from the participle stem of Latin opīnārī.

parole.significato: To express an opinion; to state as an opinion; to suppose, consider (that).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French opiner, from Latin opīnor (“to hold as an opinion”), from *opīnus (“thinking, expecting”), only in negative nec-opīnus (“not expecting”) and in-opīnus (“not expected”); akin to optō (“to choose, desire”), and to apīscor (“to obtain”); see optate and opt.

parole.significato: A chance for advancement, progress or profit.
parole.testo: From opportune + -ity, from Middle French opportunité, from Latin opportūnitās.

parole.significato: Causing opprobrium; offensive and shameful.
parole.testo: From Middle English opprobrious, from Middle French opprobrieux and its etymon Late Latin opprobriōsus.

parole.significato: To contradict or controvert; to oppose; to challenge or question the truth or validity of a given statement.
parole.testo: From Middle French oppugner Latin oppugno (“fight against, to attack, assail, assault, storm, besiege, war with”).

parole.significato: Expressing a wish or a choice.
parole.testo: From Middle French optatif, from Late Latin optātīvus, a calque of Ancient Greek εὐκτική (euktikḗ, “related to wishing”), from Latin optātus, past participle of optāre.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the eye or to vision.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French optique or Medieval Latin opticus, from Ancient Greek ὀπτῐκός (optĭkós, “of or for sight”), from ὀπτός (optós, “visible”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “-ic”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: A small or petty work.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French opuscule, from Latin opusculum, diminutive of opus. Compare opuscle, opusculum. Equivalent to opus + -cule.

parole.significato: The gold or yellow tincture on a coat of arms.
parole.testo: From late Middle English or (“gold”), borrowed from Middle French or (“yellow”), from Old French or, from Latin aurum (“gold”). Doublet of aurum.

parole.significato: The act of ordaining or the state of being ordained.
parole.testo: From Middle French ordination, from Old French ordinacion, from Latin ordinatio.

parole.significato: A musician who plays the organ.
parole.testo: From Middle French organiste, from Medieval Latin organista. By surface analysis, organ + -ist.

parole.significato: The quality of being organized.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French organisation, from Medieval Latin organizātiō; by surface analysis, organize + -ation.

parole.significato: To arrange in working order.
parole.testo: From Middle English organizen, organysen, partly from Middle French organiser and partly from its etymon, Medieval Latin organizō, from Latin organum (“organ”). By surface analysis, organ + -ize.

parole.significato: A mouth or aperture, such as of a tube, pipe, etc.; an opening.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Old French, from Late Latin ōrificium (“an opening, literally the making of a mouth”), compound of ōs (“mouth”) + faciō (“to make”).

parole.significato: Any of various colourful passerine birds, New World orioles of the genus Icterus (family Icteridae) and Old World oriol…
parole.testo: A borrowing from Middle French oriol, from Old French oriol, from Latin aureolus, diminutive of aureus (“golden”). Doublet of aureole. First use appears c. 1776 in the writings of Thomas Pennant.

parole.significato: Conforming to the accepted, established, or traditional doctrines of a given faith, religion, or ideology.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English orthodoxe, from Middle French orthodoxe and its etymon Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”). Displaced native Old English wuldorlīċ.

parole.significato: Of two objects, at right angles; perpendicular to each other.
parole.testo: From Middle French orthogonal, in turn from Medieval Latin orthogōnālis and Latin orthogōnius (“right-angled”), ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀρθογώνιος (orthogṓnios, “rectangular”). By surface analysis, ortho- + -gon + -al.

parole.significato: A small European migratory bunting (Emberiza hortulana), once eaten whole as a delicacy.
parole.testo: From Middle French hortolan (“gardener”), from Latin hortulānus (“gardener”). Doublet of hortulan.

parole.significato: Either of the horn-like protuberances on the heads of giraffes and male okapi. Some extinct species in the family bore…
parole.testo: From Latin os (“bone”) and Middle French cone, from Latin cōnus (“cone, wedge, peak”), from Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos, “cone, spinning top, pine cone”).

parole.significato: Gypaetus barbatus, the bearded vulture, the diet of which is almost exclusively bone marrow.
parole.testo: From Middle French ossifrage, from Latin ossifraga (“osprey”), ossifragus (“osprey”), from ossifragus (“bone breaking”).

parole.significato: The act of presenting an ostensive definition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ostension, in turn from Latin ostensiō, ostensiōnem.

parole.significato: Apparently true, but not necessarily; ostensible
parole.testo: From Middle French ostensif and its etymon Late Latin ostēnsīvus.

parole.significato: To make an ambitious display of; to exhibit or show boastingly; to ostentate.
parole.testo: From Middle French ostenter (“to make an ostentatious display of”), or directly from its etymon Latin ostentāre (“to exhibit, present, show; to show off”), frequentative of ostendere (“to exhibit, show”), from ob- (prefix meaning ‘against; towards’) + tendere (“to extend, stretch; to distend”) (from

parole.significato: A portent, a token.
parole.testo: From Middle French ostente (“amazing or marvellous thing; prodigy, wonder”) or directly from its etymon Latin ostentum (“portent”), from ostendere (“to exhibit, show”); see further at etymology 1. The plural form ostenta is from Latin ostenta.

parole.significato: Ambitious display; vain show; display intended to excite admiration or applause.
parole.testo: Originated 1425–75 from late Middle English ostentacioun, borrowed from Middle French ostentation and its etymon Latin ostentātiō, ostentātiōnem, equivalent to ostentātus (past participle of ostentāre, to display or exhibit), frequentative of ostendere (“to present, display”) + -iōn. By surface anal

parole.significato: The state or quality of being otiose.
parole.testo: From otiose + -ity, from Middle French ociosité, from Latin otiositas, from Latin otiosus + -itas (“-ity”).

parole.significato: An avoirdupois ounce, weighing ¹⁄₁₆ of an avoirdupois pound, or 28.349523125 grams.
parole.testo: From Middle English ounce, unce, from Middle French once, from Latin ū̆ncia (“Roman ounce, various similar units”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one”). Doublet of a, one, inch, uncia, onça, onza, oka, ouguiya, and awqiyyah.

parole.significato: To bring peace to (a place or situation), by ending (or suppressing) war, fighting, violence, anger or agitation.
parole.testo: From Middle French pacifier, from Latin pāx (“peace”) + faciō (“to do, make”). Cognate with pay and peacify.

parole.significato: An agreement; a compact; a covenant.
parole.testo: From Middle English pact, from Middle French pacte, from Old French, and its etymon Latin pactum (“something agreed upon”), from pacīscī (“to agree”).

parole.significato: To mark or number the pages of, as a book or manuscript.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French page, from Latin pāgina, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-. Doublet of pagina.

parole.significato: Rebirth; regeneration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, French palingénésie, from Late Latin palingenesia: see further at palingenesis.

parole.significato: An ode or other poem in which the author retracts something said in an earlier poem; (loosely) a recantation.
parole.testo: From Middle French palinod, from Latin palinōdia (“palinode, recantation”), from Ancient Greek παλινῳδία (palinōidía, “palinode”), from πάλιν (pálin, “again”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

parole.significato: A narrow vertical stripe, narrower than a pale. Diminutive of pale.
parole.testo: Said to be from Middle English *palet, from Middle French *palet, from Middle French pal (“pale”), ultimately from Latin palla (“a strip of cloth”).

parole.significato: The alleviation of a disease's symptoms without a cure; temporary relief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French palliation, from Latin palliare (“to cloak; to conceal”), from Latin pallium (“cloak”). By surface analysis, palliate + -ion.

parole.significato: Serving to palliate; serving to extenuate or mitigate.
parole.testo: From Middle French palliatif, from New Latin *palliātīvus, from Medieval Latin palliō (“to cloak”), from Latin pallium (“a cloak”).

parole.significato: Capable of being touched, felt or handled; touchable, tangible.
parole.testo: From Middle French palpable and its source, Latin palpābilis, which is from palpō (“to touch softly”) + -bilis.

parole.significato: An abnormal beating of the heart that may be perceived by the patient, a result of excitement, exertion, or illness.
parole.testo: From Middle French palpitation, from Latin palpitatio.

parole.significato: A small, brief printed work, consisting either of a folded sheet of paper, or several sheets bound together into a book…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English pamflet, pamphilet (“short written text; small book; tract”) [and other forms], from Middle French Pamphilet (compare Late Latin (Anglo-Latin) pamfletus, panfletus, paunflettus (“short written text”), Old French Panfilès), a popular shorthand for the 12th

parole.significato: A membrane of tissue in the body of a human or animal.
parole.testo: From Middle French pannicle, and its source, Late Latin panniculus (“membrane”), from Latin panniculus (“small rag”), from pannus (“cloth”).

parole.significato: A Roman Catholic, especially one whose loyalties are seen to be with the papacy in Rome.
parole.testo: From Middle French papiste, from Latin pāpa (“pope”).

parole.significato: An apparently self-contradictory statement, which can only be true if it is false, and vice versa.
parole.testo: From Middle French paradoxe, from Latin paradoxum, from Ancient Greek παράδοξος (parádoxos, “unexpected, strange”).

parole.significato: A passage in text that starts on a new line, the first line sometimes being indented, and usually marks a change of top…
parole.testo: From Middle English paragraf, from Middle French paragraphe from Latin paragraphus (“sign for start of a new section of discourse”), from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos), from παρά (pará, “beside”) and γράφω (gráphō, “to write”). Doublet of paragraphos.

parole.significato: Equally distant from one another at all points.
parole.testo: From Middle French parallèle and its etymon Latin parallēlus, parallēlos. The verb is from the noun. See also para- and allo-.

parole.significato: A fallacious argument or illogical conclusion, especially one committed by mistake, or believed by the speaker to be lo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French paralogisme, from Late Latin paralogismus, from Ancient Greek παραλογισμός (paralogismós).

parole.significato: A friend of the bridegroom; a best man; a bridesmaid.
parole.testo: From Middle French paranymphe, from Latin paranymphus, from Ancient Greek παράνυμφος (paránumphos, “friend of bridegroom”), from παρα- (para-, “para-”) + νύμφη (númphē, “bride”).

parole.significato: A restatement of a text in different words, often to clarify meaning or from memory rather than verbatim.
parole.testo: From Middle French paraphrase, from Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis), equivalent to para- + phrase. Doublet of paraphrasis.

parole.significato: An organism that lives on or in another organism of a different species, deriving benefit from living on or in that oth…
parole.testo: From Middle French parasite, from Latin parasitus, from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos, “person who eats at the table of another”), from noun use of adjective meaning "feeding beside", from παρά (pará, “beside”) + σῖτος (sîtos, “food”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a parent.
parole.testo: From Middle French parental, from Latin parentālis, from parens (“parent”).

parole.significato: A native, citizen and/or inhabitant of Paris, France
parole.testo: From Middle English Parisien, perisien, from Middle French parisien, from Medieval Latin parisiānus. By surface analysis, Paris + -ian.

parole.significato: Equality; comparability of strength or intensity.
parole.testo: From Middle French parité, from Late Latin paritās, from Latin pār (“equal”). Equivalent to pari- + -ty.

parole.significato: Parley; talk.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English parlen (“to speak”), from Middle French parler, from Old French parler, from Late Latin parabolō.

parole.significato: A hard, full-fat Italian cheese from Parma or its neighboring province Reggio Emilia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French parmesan, from an earlier Vulgar Latin *parmēsānus, restructuring of Latin parmēnsis (from Latin Parma). Compare Italian parmigiano, Catalan parmesà, Portuguese parmesão, Sicilian parmisanu, Spanish parmesano

parole.significato: Word of mouth.
parole.testo: from Middle French parole, from Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parable.

parole.significato: To release (a prisoner) on the understanding that s/he checks in regularly and obeys the law.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French parole (“word, formal promise”), from Old French parole, from Late Latin parabola (“speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parabola, parable, and palaver.

parole.significato: A period (especially one of several recurring periods) during the course of an illness when symptoms worsen; a sudden a…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English paroxism, paroxisme (“period of worsening of a disease, attack; sudden recurrent fever”), from Middle French paroxisme, paroxysme, and Old French peroxime (“period of worsening of a disease; bout of fever or illness”) (modern French paroxysme), and from their etymon Late Lat

parole.significato: Someone who kills a relative, especially a parent.
parole.testo: From Middle French parricide, from Latin parricīda, of uncertain origin, perhaps from pār (“equal”).

parole.significato: The killing of a relative, especially a parent.
parole.testo: From Middle French parricide, from Latin parricīdium, of uncertain origin, perhaps from pār (“equal”).

parole.significato: Preference, bias in favor of, tendency.
parole.testo: From Middle English parcialite, parcialtee, parcyalte, partialte, percialite, from Middle French partialité and its etymon Medieval Latin partiālitās. Doublet of partialitas.

parole.significato: One who participates.
parole.testo: From stem of particip(ate) + -ant, borrowed from Middle French participant, from Latin participāns, present participle of participō; see participate. Displaced native Old English dǣlnimend (literally “part taker”).

parole.significato: The act of participating, of taking part in something.
parole.testo: From Middle English participacioun, from Middle French [Term?], from Old French participacion, from Late Latin participatiō. By surface analysis, participate + -ion.

parole.significato: A very small piece of matter, a fragment; especially, the smallest possible part of something.
parole.testo: From Middle French particule, and its source, Latin particula (“small part, particle”), diminutive of pars (“part, piece”). Semantically displaced native Old English grot whence modern English groat.

parole.significato: A particular thing.
parole.testo: From Middle French particularité (“part of a whole; something particular, particularity”) (modern French particularité), and from its etymon Late Latin particularitas (“fact or quality of being particular; something particular, particularity”), from Latin particulāris (“particular; partial”) + -tās

parole.significato: Being subjected to an action without producing a reaction.
parole.testo: From Middle English passyf, passyve, from Middle French, French passif, from Latin passivus (“serving to express the suffering of an action; in late Latin literally capable of suffering or feeling”), from passus, past participle of pati (“to suffer”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to shepherds or herders of other livestock.
parole.testo: From Middle French, Old French pastoral, from Latin pāstōrālis, from pāstor (“shepherd”), + adjective suffix -ālis.

parole.significato: Fatherhood, the state or quality of being a father.
parole.testo: From Middle French paternité, from Old French, from Latin paternitās (“paternity”), from paternus (“of or pertaining to a father, paternal”) + -itās, from pater (“father”).

parole.significato: Arousing pity, sympathy, or compassion; exciting pathos.
parole.testo: From Middle French pathétique, from Latin patheticus, from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós, “subject to feeling, capable of feeling, impassioned”), from παθητός (pathētós, “one who has suffered, subject to suffering”), from πάσχω (páskhō, “to suffer”). By surface analysis, path- + -etic.

parole.significato: Willing to wait if necessary; not losing one's temper while waiting.
parole.testo: From Middle English pacient, from Middle French patient, from Old French pacient, from Latin patiens, present participle of patior (“to suffer, endure”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate, hurt”).

parole.significato: A patriarchal system or community.
parole.testo: From Middle French patriarcat, from Old French patriarcat, from Medieval Latin patriarchatus, from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “patriarch”). By surface analysis, patriarch + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, the concrete charge of it, a body of people involved with it).

parole.significato: A member of any of the families constituting the populus Romanus, or body of Roman citizens, before the development of…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French patricien, from Latin patricius, derived from patrēs cōnscrīptī (“Roman senators”). May also have been derived from Latin patricius + -ian

parole.significato: The murder of one's father.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French patricide or Latin patricīdium. Equivalent to patri- + -cide.

parole.significato: One who has murdered their father.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French patricide or Latin patricīda. Equivalent to patri- + -cide.

parole.significato: A right or estate inherited from one's father; or, in a larger sense, from any male ancestor.
parole.testo: From earlier patrimoyne, from patremoyne, from Middle French patrimoine/patremoine, semilearned borrowing from Latin patrimōnium, from pater (“father”) + -mōnium (“state, condition”). First attested in 1513. By surface analysis, patri- + -mony. Compare matrimony. Displaced native Old English fæderġe

parole.significato: A person who loves and zealously supports and defends their country.
parole.testo: From Middle French patriote, from Late Latin patriōta (“fellow countryman”) from the Ancient Greek πατριώτης (patriṓtēs, “of the same country”), from πατρίς (patrís, “father land", "country”), from πατήρ (patḗr, “father”).

parole.significato: Fewness in number; too few.
parole.testo: From Middle English paucete, paucite, paucyte, partly from Middle French paucité and partly from its etymon, Latin paucitās (“a small number, fewness, scarcity”), from paucus (“few, little”). Related to few.

parole.significato: To take a temporary rest, take a break for a short period after an effort.
parole.testo: From Middle French pause, from Latin pausa, from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis), from Ancient Greek παύω (paúō, “stop”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of pausa.

parole.significato: Of a person, etc.: that commits or has committed an offence or a sin; blameworthy, culpable, offending, sinful, sinning.
parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from Middle French peccant (“unhealthy”) (modern French peccant), and from its etymon Late Latin peccantis, the genitive singular of peccāns (“offending; sinning, transgressing”, adjective), from Latin peccāns (“wrongdoer”), a noun use of the active present participle of pe

parole.significato: A teacher or instructor of children; one whose occupation is to teach the young.
parole.testo: From Middle English pedagoge, from Middle French pedagogue, from Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”) (from ἄγω (ágō, “lead”)). By surface analysis, ped- (“child”) + -agogue.

parole.significato: A legal sentence.
parole.testo: From Middle French pénalité, from pénal, from Latin poenālis, from poena, borrowing of Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ), from Proto-Hellenic *kʷoinā́, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂, comprising *kʷey- + *-néh₂.

parole.significato: To hang down; to cause something to hang down
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French pendre (“to hang”), from Late Latin pendĕre, from Latin pendēre.

parole.significato: A polygon with five sides and five angles.
parole.testo: From Middle French pentagone, from Late Latin pentagōnum, from Ancient Greek πεντάγωνον (pentágōnon), noun use of the neuter of the adjective πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos, “five-angled”), from πέντε (pénte, “five”) + -γωνος (-gōnos, “angled”). Equivalent to penta- + -gon.

parole.significato: The organisation, identification and interpretation of sensory information.
parole.testo: From Middle English percepcioun, from Middle French percepcion, from Latin perceptiō (“a receiving or collecting, perception, comprehension”), from perceptus (“perceived, observed”), perfect passive participle of percipiō (“to perceive, observe”); see perceive.

parole.significato: The collision of two bodies in order to produce a sound.
parole.testo: From Middle English percussioun, from Middle French, Old French percussion, from Latin percussiō (“striking”), from percutiō (“to strike”).

parole.significato: A state or act of violating faith or allegiance; violation of a promise or vow, or of trust.
parole.testo: From Middle French perfidie, from Latin perfidia from perfidus (“faithless, treacherous, false”), from fides (“faith”); related to, for example, English fidelity.

parole.significato: The act of perfusing, the passage of fluid through the circulatory system.
parole.testo: From Middle French perfusion, from Latin perfūsiō (“the act of pouring over”).

parole.significato: A length of time.
parole.testo: From Middle English periode, from Middle French periode, from Medieval Latin periodus, from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos, “circuit, orbit, a recurring interval of time, path around”), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way”). Displaced native Middle English tide (“interval, period, sea

parole.significato: The outside boundary, parts or surface of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French peripherie. Compare Middle English periferie (“one of three layers of atmosphere (lower, middle, and upper) believed to surround the Earth”), from the same origin, although the Modern English term most likely does not descend from it.

parole.significato: The state of being permanent.
parole.testo: From Middle English permanence, permanens, from Middle French permanence, from Medieval Latin permanentia, from Latin permaneō (“to remain; last”).

parole.significato: Without end, eternal.
parole.testo: From Middle English permanent, permanente, from Middle French permanent, from Latin permanēns, from permaneō (“to stay through”). First attested in the 15th century.

parole.significato: authorisation; consent (especially formal consent from someone in authority)
parole.testo: From Middle English permision, permission, permissioun, permyssion, from Middle French permission, from Latin permissiō. Equivalent to permit + -ion. Mostly replaced native English leave, from Old English lēaf (“permission”).

parole.significato: To allow (something) to happen, to give permission for.
parole.testo: From Middle English permitten, borrowed from Middle French permettre, from Latin permittō (“give up, allow”), from per (“through”) + mittō (“send”).

parole.significato: At or forming a right angle (to something).
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French perpendiculaire, from Old French perpendiculer, from Latin perpendiculum (“plumb line”).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being perplexed.
parole.testo: From Middle English perplexite, borrowed from Middle French perplexité or post-classical Latin perplexitās, from perplexus (“entangled”). By surface analysis, perplex + -ity.

parole.significato: To pursue in a manner to do harm or cruelty to; especially, because of the victim's race, sexual identity, or adherence…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French persécuter, from Ecclesiastical Latin persecutor, from Latin persequor, persecutus (“follow up, pursue”), from per- (“through”) + sequor (“follow”) (English sequel). Compare prosecute. Cf. also pursue.

parole.significato: Enduring; persistent, resistant.
parole.testo: From Middle English perseveraunt, from Middle French perseverant, from Latin persevērāns, present participle of persevērō.

parole.significato: To go on stubbornly or resolutely.
parole.testo: From Middle French persister (Modern French persister), from Latin persistere, from per- + sistere (“to stand”).

parole.significato: The property of being persistent.
parole.testo: From Middle French persistance, from persistant, from Latin persistēns, from persistō. By surface analysis, persist + -ence.

parole.significato: Of a person: having a pleasing appearance; attractive; handsome.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English personable, personabil (“having a pleasing appearance, handsome”), and then from both of the following: * For sense 1 (“having a pleasing appearance”) and sense 2 (“having a pleasant manner”) (these senses are not found in Old French or Medieval Latin), probably from person,

parole.significato: Of people, a set of non-physical psychological and social qualities that make one person distinct from another.
parole.testo: From Middle English personalite, from Middle French [Term?], from Latin persōnālitās. First attested in the late 14th century. By surface analysis, personal + -ity.

parole.significato: Acute discernment or understanding; insight.
parole.testo: From Middle French perspicacité (whence -acity) or directly from Latin perspicācitās (“sharpsightedness, discrimination”), from perspicāx (“sharp-sighted”), from perspicio, from per- + specio, "see through (something)".

parole.significato: The action or process of perspiring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from late Middle French perspiration, from perspirer (“perspire”), from Latin perspirare (“to blow or breathe constantly”), from per (“through”) + spirare (“to breathe, blow”). Morphologically perspire + -ation.

parole.significato: To emit (sweat or perspiration) through the skin's pores.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French perspirer and its source Latin perspīrō (“to breathe everywhere, blow constantly”), from per (“through”) + spīrō (“to breathe”); see spirit.

parole.significato: Able to persuade; convincing.
parole.testo: From Middle French persuasif, from Medieval Latin persuāsīvus, from Latin past participle stem of persuādēre + -īvus.

parole.significato: Agitation; the state of being perturbed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French perturbation, from Old French perturbacion, from Latin perturbatio.

parole.significato: The quality of being perverse.
parole.testo: From perverse + -ity, from Middle French perversité, from Latin perversitās.

parole.significato: A pestilence, i.e. a deadly epidemic, a deadly plague.
parole.testo: In the 16th century in the sense of "pestilence" and specifically bubonic plague from Middle French peste (“pestilence”) (whence French peste). The other meanings are recorded soon after. Ultimately from Latin pestis.

parole.significato: To turn to stone: to harden organic matter by permeating with water and depositing dissolved minerals.
parole.testo: From Middle French pétrifier, from Medieval Latin petrificāre, from Latin petra (“rock”), from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “rock”) + -ficāre, from facere (“do, make”), equivalent to petro- + -ify.

parole.significato: A short but large-caliber, heavy 16th- and 17th-century firearm that used a matchlock or wheellock mechanism, intermedi…
parole.testo: From Middle French petrinal, alteration of poitrinal, from poitrinal (“of the chest”) (the weapon is thought to have been braced against a chest-pad when firing), from poitrine (“chest, breast”), from Latin pectorina, feminine of pectorinus (“of the breast”) (from pectus (“chest”) + -inus (“-ine”)).

parole.significato: Resembling rock or stone in its hardness.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French petreux, from Latin petrōsus, from petra, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra).

parole.significato: Rudeness, insolence.
parole.testo: From Middle French pétulance, and its source, Latin petulantia.

parole.significato: Childishly irritable.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Latin petulāns, akin to petō (“to ask for”).

parole.significato: Synonym of phalanx (“group of soldiers, people etc.”).
parole.testo: From Middle English phalange, from Middle French phalange, from Old French phalange, from Latin phalanx (accusative phalangem), from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx). Doublet of phalanx, planch, plancha, planche, and plank.

parole.significato: A place where prescription drugs are sold or dispensed.
parole.testo: From Middle English pharmacy, borrowed from Middle French pharmacie (“the art of creating drugs; a drug, especially a laxative”), from Old French farmacie, from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”), from φάρμακον (phármakon, “a drug, charm, enchantm

parole.significato: A bottle or other vessel for containing a liquid; originally any such vessel, especially one for holding a beverage; no…
parole.testo: The noun is derived partly: * from Middle English fiole, phiole, phial (“small bowl or cup for liquids, etc.; flask”) [and other forms], from Middle French fiole, phiole [and other forms], and Old French fiole (modern French fiole), from Late Latin fiola, phiola, from Latin phiala (“broad, flat, sha

parole.significato: A philologist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French philologue, from Latin philologus (“lover of learning”), from Ancient Greek φιλολόγος (philológos, “lover of words and learning”). Equivalent to philo- + -logue.

parole.significato: Reverence and devotion to God.
parole.testo: From Middle English piete, borrowed from Middle French pieté, from Latin pietās. See also the doublets pietà and pity. By surface analysis, pious + -ety.

parole.significato: A large farm; estate or area of land designated for agricultural growth. Often includes housing for the owner and worke…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French plantation, from Latin plantātiō (“planting, transplanting”), from plantātus (“planted”), the perfect passive participle of plantāre, + action noun suffix -tiō.

parole.significato: An act of folding.
parole.testo: From Middle French plicacion, and its source, Latin plicatio.

parole.significato: The feathers covering the body of a bird collectively.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English plumage, plummage (“bird’s feathers collectively, plumage; (falconry) feathers fed to a hawk to cause it to regurgitate, casting”), from Middle French plumage, plomage (“bird’s feathers collectively; person’s (showy) clothing”), from Old French plumage (“bird’s feathers coll

parole.significato: A literary piece written in verse.
parole.testo: From Middle French poème, from Latin poēma, from Ancient Greek ποίημα (poíēma), from ποιέω (poiéō, “to make”). Widely displaced English leed.

parole.significato: A poem.
parole.testo: From Middle English poesie (Middle English po(esie) + -esy), from Middle French poesie, from Late Latin poesia, from earlier poēsis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis). Doublet of poiesis.

parole.significato: Relating to poetry.
parole.testo: From Middle French poetique, from Latin poeticus, from Ancient Greek ποιητικός (poiētikós) from ποιέω (poiéō, “make”). Displaced native Old English sċoplīċ and lēoþlīċ. Doublet of poietic.

parole.significato: Either of the two points on the earth's surface around which it rotates; also, similar points on any other rotating obj…
parole.testo: From Middle French pole, pôle, from Latin polus, from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, “axis of rotation”).

parole.significato: The pole star.
parole.testo: From pole + arctic, after Middle French pôle arctique, Late Latin polus arcticus.

parole.significato: To enforce the law and keep order among (a group).
parole.testo: From Middle French police, from Latin polītīa (“state, government”), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía). Doublet of policy, polis (“police”), and polity.

parole.significato: Of or relating to polity, or civil government; political.
parole.testo: From Middle French politique, from Latin polīticus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”). Cognate with German politisch (“political”). Doublet of politico.

parole.significato: Organizational structure and governance, especially of a state or a religion.
parole.testo: From Middle French politie, from Latin polītīa, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, “polity, policy, the state”). Doublet of police, policy, and polis (“police”).

parole.significato: A dagger typically having a slender square or triangular blade.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French poignard (whence -ard), from poing (“fist”), from Old French poing, from Latin pugnus (“fist”).

parole.significato: A member of the most illustrious of the colleges of priests of the Roman religion, the College of Pontiffs; a pontifex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French pontife m, from Latin pontifex m. Doublet of pontifex.

parole.significato: A flat-bottomed boat or other floating structure used as a buoyant support for a temporary bridge, dock or landing stag…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ponton, from Old French ponton, from Latin pontō, pontōnem (“ferryboat”), from pōns (“bridge”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or being a pig.
parole.testo: From Middle English porcine, partly from Middle French porcin (from Old French [Term?]) and partly from its etymon, Latin porcīnus, from porcus (“pig”).

parole.significato: Able to be carried or easily moved.
parole.testo: From Middle English portable, from Middle French portable and Latin portābilis. By surface analysis, port (“to carry”) + -able.

parole.significato: An act of carrying, especially the carrying of a boat overland between two waterways.
parole.testo: From Middle English portage, borrowed from Middle French portage, from Old French portage, from Early Medieval Latin portāticum. By surface analysis, port (“to carry”) + -age.

parole.significato: The manner in which one carries oneself; behaviour.
parole.testo: From Middle French portance (“a carrying, support”), from porter (“to carry”), from Latin portare (“carry, bear, convey”).

parole.significato: A Portuguese person.
parole.testo: From Middle English Portyngale, from Middle French Portingal, which added an intrusive /n/ sound through the process of excrescence, from Latin Portucale.

parole.significato: A large travelling case usually made of leather, and opening into two equal sections.
parole.testo: From Middle French portemanteau (“coat stand”), from porte (“he carries”, third-person singular present indicative of porter (“to carry”)) + manteau (“coat”), literally “[that which] carries coat”. The lexical sense (sense 2) was first used figuratively by Lewis Carroll in Through the Looking-Glass

parole.significato: A painting or other picture of a person, especially the head and shoulders.
parole.testo: From Middle French portraict, pourtraict, nominal use of the past participle of portraire (“portray”), from Latin prōtrahō (< prō- + trahō). Compare typologically English drawing.

parole.significato: To have (something) as, or as if as, an owner; to have, to own.
parole.testo: PIE word  *pótis From Middle English possessen (“to have, own; to obtain possession of; to inhabit, occupy”) [and other forms], from Middle French possesser, possessier, Old French possesser, possessier (“to have, own, possess; to dominate”), from Latin possessus (“possessed; seized”), the perfect p

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to ownership or possession.
parole.testo: From Middle French possessif, from Latin possessivus (“of or pertaining to possession”), from possessiō (“possessing”), from possidēre (“to possess”). By surface analysis, possess + -ive.

parole.significato: The quality of being possible.
parole.testo: From Middle English possibilite, from Middle French possibilité (from Old French possibilite) and directly from Late Latin possibilitās (“possibility”), from Latin possibilis (“possible”); see possible. By surface analysis, possible + -ity.

parole.significato: All the future generations, especially the descendants of a specific person.
parole.testo: Late 14th century, from Middle French posterité, from Latin posteritas, from posterus (“following, coming after”), from post (“after”) (English post-).

parole.significato: Good for drinking without fear of waterborne disease or poisoning.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English potable (“drinkable, potable”), from Middle French, Old French potable (modern French potable (“drinkable, potable”)), and from its etymon Late Latin pōtābilis (“drinkable, potable”), from Latin pōtāre (“to drink”) + -bilis (suffix forming adjectives

parole.significato: Power or strength; potency.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French potence (“power, a crutch”), from Latin potentia (“power, in Medieval Latin also crutch”), from potens (“powerful”); see potent.

parole.significato: Repetition of an activity to improve a skill.
parole.testo: The noun is from Middle English practice, practique, practyse, from the verb; also compare Medieval Latin prāctica.. Displaced native Old English sidu. The verb is from Middle English practice, practise, practize, practyse, from Middle French pratiser, practiser, alteration of practiquer, from Medie

parole.significato: To repeat (an activity) as a way of improving one's skill in that activity.
parole.testo: From Middle English practizen, a variant of practisen, from Middle French pratiser, practiser, from Medieval Latin practizo, from Late Latin practico (“to do, perform, execute, propose, practise, exercise, be conversant with, contrive, conspire, etc.”), from prāctica (“practical affairs", "business”

parole.significato: Practical, concerned with making decisions and actions that are useful in practice, not just theory.
parole.testo: From Middle French pragmatique, from Late Latin pragmaticus (“relating to civil affair; in Latin, as a noun, a person versed in the law who furnished arguments and points to advocates and orators, a kind of attorney”), from Ancient Greek πραγματικός (pragmatikós, “active, versed in affairs”), from π

parole.significato: A green gem; an emerald.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from a combination of Middle French prame (inherited from Late Latin prasinus) and Middle French prasine (borrowed from Late Latin prasinum), both ultimately from Latin prasinus (“leek-green”), from Ancient Greek πράσινος (prásinos), from πράσον (práson, “leek”).

parole.significato: Permission to use a port given to a ship after compliance with quarantine or on conviction that she is free of contagio…
parole.testo: Originated 1600–10. Borrowed from Middle French practique, pratique, from Medieval Latin prāctica. Doublet of practice.

parole.significato: Perversion, depravity; wickedness.
parole.testo: From Middle French pravité, and its source, Latin prāvitās (“crookedness; depravity”), from prāvus (“prave”).

parole.significato: A stipend paid to a canon of a cathedral.
parole.testo: From Middle French prebende, from Medieval Latin prebenda, from Late Latin praebenda, from Latin praebendus, verbal adjective of praebere. Doublet of provender.

parole.significato: To go before, go in front of.
parole.testo: From Middle French précéder, from Latin praecēdō, from prae- + cēdō.

parole.significato: An act in the past which may be used as an example to help decide the outcome of similar instances in the future.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Old French, from Latin praecēdēns, present participle of praecēdere (“to precede”); See precede.

parole.significato: The quality of being overly refined in an affected way (often used to describe speech or writing, but also visual art a…
parole.testo: From Middle English preciosite, from Middle French preciosité, from Latin pretiōsitās (“great value; high price”).

parole.significato: A very steep cliff.
parole.testo: First attested in 1598, from Middle French precipice, from Latin praecipitium (“a steep place”), from praeceps (“steep”), from prae + caput (“head”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“head”). Distantly related to precept through Latin praecipiō (“to teach”), from prae + capiō (“take”), ult

parole.significato: Inclined to make rapid decisions without due consideration; hasty, impulsive, rash.
parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from Middle French précipitant, Old French precipitant (“acting hastily, hasty, rash; acting, happening, or moving rapidly; pressing”) (modern French précipitant), and from their etymon Late Latin praecipitans (“hasty, rash”), an adjective use of Latin praecipitāns, the pre

parole.significato: Any or all of the forms of water particles, whether liquid or solid, that fall from the upper atmosphere (e.g., rain, h…
parole.testo: From Middle French précipitation, from Latin praecipitātiō, praecipitātiōnem. By surface analysis, precipitate + -ion.

parole.significato: Both exact and accurate.
parole.testo: From Middle French précis, from Latin praecīsus, perfect passive participle of praecīdere, from prae- (“before, in front”) + caedere (“cut; strike”), cognate with hit. Related to incise. Doublet of précis.

parole.significato: Knowledge of the future; understanding of something in advance, especially as a form of supernatural or extrasensory pe…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French precognition or its source, Latin praecognitio, from praecognōscō (“to know beforehand”). Doublet of Germanic-based foreknowledge and Greek-based prognosis. Equivalent to pre- + cognition.

parole.significato: That which precurses: a forerunner, predecessor, or indicator of approaching events.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English precursour, from Middle French precurseur or its etymon Latin praecursor (“forerunner”). By surface analysis, precurse + -or.

parole.significato: Common or widespread; prevalent.
parole.testo: From Middle French prédominant, ultimately from Medieval Latin praedominans. By surface analysis, pre- + dominant.

parole.significato: Exceeding others in quality or rank; of outstanding excellence, extremely notable or important.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French preeminent and its source, Latin praeēminēns, present participle of praeēmineō (“to stand out, excel”), from prae- (“pre-”) + ēmineō.

parole.significato: The office or position of a prefect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French préfecture, from Latin praefectūra. Equivalent to prefect + -ure. As an East Asian administrative division, a calque of Chinese 府 (fǔ) and 郡 (jùn), also used to describe 縣 /县 (xian, “county”) and 州 (zhou, “province”) in some eras.

parole.significato: The selection of one thing or person over others (with the main adposition being "for" in relation to the thing or pers…
parole.testo: From Middle French preference, from Medieval Latin preferentia. Doublet of preferans. Morphologically prefer + -ence. Compare typologically Russian предвзя́тость (predvzjátostʹ) (<< взять (vzjatʹ), a suppletive of брать (bratʹ), which is cognate with Latin ferō).

parole.significato: To determine beforehand; to set in advance.
parole.testo: From Middle English prefixen, from Middle French prefixer, from Latin praefīxus, past participle of praefīgō (“to (fix, fasten, set up) in front”, “to fix on the (end, extremity)”) (from prae- (“before”) + fīgō (“to fix”, “to fasten”, “to affix”)), equivalent to pre- + -fix.

parole.significato: Compelling; clear, evident.
parole.testo: Apparently from Middle French pregnant, preignant (“pressing, compelling”), present participle of prembre (“to press”), from Latin premere (“to press”).

parole.significato: Existing previously, preexistent.
parole.testo: Multiple origins. Borrowed from Middle French prejacent (“previously existing”) during the sixteenth century. Also attested in twelfth century British sources, from post-classical Latin praeiacens (“situated before”).

parole.significato: To form a judgment of (something) in advance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French préjuger, itself an adaptation of Latin praeudico, praeiudicare. Doublet of prejudicate.

parole.significato: An introductory or preliminary performance or event.
parole.testo: From Middle French prélude (“singing to test a musical instrument”), from Medieval Latin preludium, from Latin praelūdere.

parole.significato: Foremost; first or highest in quality or degree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French premier (adjective), from Latin prīmārius. Doublet of primary.

parole.significato: The state of being preoccupied or an idea that preoccupies the mind; enthrallment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French préoccupation, from Latin praeoccupātiō. By surface analysis, pre- + occupation or preoccupy + -ation.

parole.significato: To distract; to draw attention elsewhere.
parole.testo: From pre- + occupy, after Middle French preoccuper, and its source, Latin praeoccupo, praeoccupare. Doublet of preoccupate, now obsolete.

parole.significato: The act of preparing or getting ready.
parole.testo: From Middle English preparacion, from Middle French preparacion, from Latin praeparatio, praeparationem. Morphologically prepare + -ation.

parole.significato: That serves to prepare something
parole.testo: From Middle English preperatif, from Middle French preparatif and Medieval Latin prēparātīvus.

parole.significato: To make ready for a specific future purpose; to set up; to assemble or equip; to forearm.
parole.testo: Partially a back-formation from preparation; and partially borrowed from Middle French preparer, from Classical Latin praeparāre (“make ready in advance”), from prae- (“pre-”) + parāre (“make ready”). Compare Middle English preparaten (“to prepare”).

parole.significato: A written order from an authorized medical practitioner for provision of a medicine or other treatment, such as (ophtha…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French prescripcion, from Latin praescriptio (“preface; pretext; something written ahead of time”), from prae- (“pre-, before”) + scribere (“to write”) + -tio (“-tion, forming nouns”). Equivalent to prescribe + -tion.

parole.significato: Belonging to a province, or being like a province; provincial.
parole.testo: From Middle French presidial, from Latin praesidialis, variant of praesidalis, from praeses (“provincial governor”).

parole.significato: To assume some truth without proof, usually for the purpose of reaching a conclusion based on that truth.
parole.testo: From Middle French presupposer, from Latin praesuppōnō.

parole.significato: An assumption made beforehand; a preliminary conjecture or speculation.
parole.testo: From Middle French présupposition, from Latin praesuppositio, from the past participle stem of praesuppōnere (“to presuppose”).

parole.significato: The action of pretending; false or simulated show or appearance; false or hypocritical assertion or representation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French pretensse, from Late Latin praetēnsus, past participle of Latin praetendō (“to pretend”), from prae- (“before”) + tendō (“to stretch”); see pretend.

parole.significato: Unspoiled; still with its original purity; uncorrupted or unsullied.
parole.testo: From Middle French pristin, borrowed from Latin prīstinus.

parole.significato: The state of being deprived of or lacking an attribute formerly or properly possessed; the loss or absence of such an a…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English privacioun, from Middle French privation, privacion, from Old French privacion, from Latin prīvātiō; compare French privation. See private.

parole.significato: The state of being probable.
parole.testo: From Middle French probabilité, from Latin probābilitās (“probability, credibility”), from probābilis (“probable, credible”).

parole.significato: A period of time when a person occupies a position only conditionally and may be removed if certain conditions are not…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English probacioun, from Middle French probation, from Old French probacion, from Latin probatio (“a trying, inspection, examination”), from probare, past participle probatus (“to test, examine”); see probate, probe, prove.

parole.significato: Integrity, especially of the quality of having strong moral principles; decency and honesty.
parole.testo: From Middle French probité, from Latin probitās (“uprightness, honesty”), from probus (“good, excellent, honest”); see probe, prove.

parole.significato: A difficulty that has to be resolved or dealt with.
parole.testo: From Middle English probleme, from Middle French probleme, from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “anything thrown forward, hindrance, obstacle, anything projecting, a headland, promontory”), from προβάλλω (probállō, “to throw or lay something in front of someone, to put forward

parole.significato: Posing a problem; having or suffering from problem(s):
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French problématique, from Late Latin problematicus, from Ancient Greek προβληματικός (problēmatikós), from πρόβλημα (próblēma, “outjutting, barrier, problem”), from προβάλλω (probállō, “I throw, place before”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + βάλλω (bállō, “I throw, place”). By surf

parole.significato: The state of being procacious; forwardness, pertness, or petulance, or an instance thereof.
parole.testo: From Middle French procacité, from Latin procācitās (whence -acity), from Latin procāx (“bold, impudent”), from procō (“ask, demand”), from procus (“suitor”).

parole.significato: A storm, a tempest.
parole.testo: From Middle French procelle, from Latin procella (“storm”), from procello (“to throw violently forward”), from pro- (“pro-: forward”) + cello (“to rise, to tower”).

parole.significato: The act of postponing, delaying or putting off, especially habitually or intentionally.
parole.testo: From Middle French procrastination, from Latin prōcrāstinātiō, from prōcrāstinō (“procrastinate”), from prō + crāstinus (“of tomorrow”), from crās (“tomorrow”).

parole.significato: The act of procuring; procurement.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English procuracioun, from Middle French procuration and its etymon Latin prōcūrātiōnem (through Old French procuracion). By surface analysis, procure + -ation; compare procuracy and procuratory.

parole.significato: Wastefully extravagant.
parole.testo: From Middle French prodigal, from Late Latin prōdigālis (“wasteful”), from Latin prōdigus (“wasteful, lavish, prodigal”), from prōdigō (“to consume, squander, drive forth”), from prōd- [from prō (“before, forward”)] + agō (“to drive”). Also see unrelated prodigy. The senses of "abandoning a person o

parole.significato: The act of profaning; desecration, blasphemous behaviour, defilement.
parole.testo: From Middle French prophanation, profanation, and its source, Late Latin profanatio, from the participle stem of Latin profānō. By surface analysis, profane + -ation.

parole.significato: Unclean; ritually impure; unholy, desecrating a holy place or thing.
parole.testo: From Middle English prophane, from Middle French profane, prophaine, prophane and its etymon Classical Latin profānus (“not religious, unclean”) (also Late Latin prophānus), from pro- (“instead of”) + fānum (“temple”).

parole.significato: To violate (something sacred); to treat with abuse, irreverence, obloquy, or contempt; to desecrate
parole.testo: From Middle English prophanen, from Middle French profaner, prophaner and its etymon Classical Latin profānō (also Late Latin prophāno), from profānus + -ō (suffix forming verbs).

parole.significato: The person who proposes a contract (or one of its clauses)
parole.testo: From Middle French proference, from Medieval Latin proferentia. Doublet of proferans.

parole.significato: The state of being profound; magnitude, gravity, or intensity.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English profundite, from Middle French profondite or its etymon Latin profunditās; by surface analysis, prof(o)und + ity. Compare profoundness.

parole.significato: abundance; the state of being profuse; a cornucopia
parole.testo: From Middle French profusion, from Late Latin profusio.

parole.significato: Favouring or promoting progress; advanced.
parole.testo: From the Middle French progressif, from the Latin prōgressīvus, from prōgredior (perfect participial stem: prōgress-) + -īvus. Displaced native Old English forþgenġe. By surface analysis, progress + -ive.

parole.significato: Quick; acting without delay.
parole.testo: The adjective is from Middle English prompte, from Middle French prompt and its etymon Latin prōmptus (“visible, apparent, evident”), past participle of prōmō (“to take or bring out or forth, produce, bring to light”), from prō (“forth, forward”) + emō (“to take, acquire, buy”). Doublet of pronto. T

parole.significato: The act of promulgating or announcing something, especially a proclamation announcing a new law.
parole.testo: From Middle French promulgation, from Latin prōmulgātiō.

parole.significato: A part of speech that refers anaphorically to a noun or noun phrase, which cannot ordinarily be preceded by a determine…
parole.testo: From pro- + noun, modeled on Middle French pronom, from Latin pronomen, itself a calque of Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ντωνῠμῐ́ᾱ (ăntōnŭmĭ́ā).

parole.significato: The way in which a word, phrase, letter, character etc. is made to sound when spoken.
parole.testo: From Middle English pronunciacioun, from Middle French prononciation, pronunciation, from Latin prōnūntiātiō, noun of action from perfect passive participle prōnūntiātus, from verb prōnūntiāre (“proclaim”), from prō- (“for”) + nūntiāre (“announce”). Doublet of pronuntiatio.

parole.significato: The multiplication or natural increase in a population.
parole.testo: From Middle French propagation, from Old French propagacion, from Latin propagatio. Morphologically propagate + -ion.

parole.significato: Having the ability to prophesize; prescient.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French prophétique, from Latin prophēticus, from Ancient Greek προφητικός (prophētikós), equivalent to prophet + -ic.

parole.significato: Nearness or proximity
parole.testo: From propinqu(ent) + -ity, from Middle English propinquite, from Middle French propinquité or Latin propinquitās, from propinquus (“neighbouring”) (from prop(e) (“near”) + (h)inc (“hence”) + -uus).

parole.significato: Pertaining to or having the characteristics of prose.
parole.testo: From Middle French prosaïque, from Medieval Latin prosaicus (“in prose”), from Latin prosa (“prose”), from prorsus (“straightforward, in prose”), from Old Latin provorsus (“straight ahead”), from pro- (“forward”) + vorsus (“turned”), from vertō (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to turn,

parole.significato: The act of prosecuting a scheme or endeavor.
parole.testo: Equivalent to prosecute + -ion, from Middle French prosecution, from Late Latin prōsecutio, from Latin prōsequor (“follow, pursue”), from pro- (“onward”) + sequor (“follow”) (English sequel). Compare persecution, and see more at prosecute.

parole.significato: A verse used in prosodia, having three anapests, of which the first may be substituted with a spondee or iamb.
parole.testo: From Middle French prosodiaque and its etymon Late Latin prosōdiacus, from Koine Greek προσοδιακός (prosodiakós), from Ancient Greek προσόδιον (prosódion) + -ακός (-akós). By surface analysis, prosodi(on) + -ac.

parole.significato: The study of rhythm, intonation, stress, and related attributes in speech.
parole.testo: From Middle French prosodie, from Latin prosōdia, from Ancient Greek προσῳδία (prosōidía, “song sung to music; pronunciation of syllable”), from πρός (prós, “to”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

parole.significato: Likely or expected to happen or become.
parole.testo: From Middle French prospectif, from Late Latin prospectivus. See more at English prospect.

parole.significato: Characterized by success.
parole.testo: From Middle French prospereus, from Old French prosperer, from Latin prosperō (“to cause to succeed”), from Old Latin pro spere (“according to expectation”), from pro (“for”) + spes (“hope”).

parole.significato: The prostate gland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French prostate, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin prostata.

parole.significato: The act or condition of prostrating oneself (lying face-down), as a sign of humility.
parole.testo: From Middle English prostracioun, prostracyon, from Middle French prostration and its etymon Latin prōstrātiō, from prōstrātus, past participle of prōsternō. By surface analysis, prostrate + -ion.

parole.significato: The minutes, or official record, of a negotiation or transaction; especially a document drawn up officially which forms…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French protocolle, protocole (“document, record”), from Late Latin protocollum (“the first sheet of a volume (on which contents and errata were written)”), from Byzantine Greek πρωτόκολλον (prōtókollon, “first sheet glued onto a manuscript”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”) + κόλλ

parole.significato: Any of the first Christian martyrs.
parole.testo: From Middle English prothomartir, prothomartyr, from Middle French prothomartir and Medieval Latin prōtomartyr, from Koine Greek πρωτομάρτυς (prōtomártus). By surface analysis, proto- + martyr.

parole.significato: Created first; archetypal.
parole.testo: From Middle French prothoplaste, and its source Late Latin protoplastus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πρωτόπλαστος (prōtóplastos, “first-formed”), from Ancient Greek πρωτο- (prōto-) + πλαστός (plastós, “formed, moulded”).

parole.significato: To originate, stem (from)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French provenir, from Latin prōvenīre.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Provence, a traditional geographic region roughly corresponding to the modern administrative re…
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Middle French provenceal, provençal, from Latin prōvinciālis.

parole.significato: Serving or tending to elicit a strong, often negative sentiment in another person; exasperating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French provocatif, and its source, Late Latin provocativus, from Latin provocare.

parole.significato: One who engages in provocation.
parole.testo: Partly borrowed from Middle French provocateur and its etymon Latin prōvocātor, and partly from provocate + -or. Doublet of provocateur.

parole.significato: To cause someone to become annoyed or angry.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French provoquer, from Old French, from Latin prōvocāre. Doublet of provocate.

parole.significato: Closeness; the state of being near in space, time, or relationship.
parole.testo: From proxim(ate) + -ity, from Middle French proximité, from Latin proximitās, proximitāt-, from proximus.

parole.significato: The study of the origins and development of the soul or mind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French psychogonie, from Late Latin psychogonia, from Koine Greek ψυχογονία (psukhogonía), from ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul, mind”) + γόνος (gónos, “descent”). By surface analysis, psycho- + -gony.

parole.significato: At or just after the age of puberty.
parole.testo: From Middle French pubescent, from Latin pubescens (“to become hairy, downy, or an adult”).

parole.significato: Modesty; chastity.
parole.testo: From Middle French pudicité, and its source, Latin pudicitia, from pudicus (“modest”).

parole.significato: The state, quality, or condition of being childish or puerile.
parole.testo: From Middle English puerilite, from Middle French puérilité and its etymon Latin puerīlitās, from puerīlis (“childish, juvenile”), from puer (“boy”). By surface analysis, puerile + -ity.

parole.significato: The regular throbbing of the heart, an artery etc. in a living body; the pulse.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pulsacioun (“pulsing of the blood, throbbing”), borrowed from Middle French pulsacion (“(of bells) a striking (end of 14th c.); (of a diseased part of the body) a throbbing (1377); pulsation (1575)”), and its source, Latin pulsātiō (“(classical Latin) a beating or strik

parole.significato: Characterised by pulsing or beating; throbbing.
parole.testo: From Middle French pulsatif, and its source, past-classical Latin pulsativus.

parole.significato: A domesticated plant, in species Cucurbita pepo, similar in growth pattern, foliage, flower, and fruit to the squash or…
parole.testo: Alteration of pompion, pumpion (“pumpkin”) with the diminutive -kin, from Middle French pompon, from Latin pepō (whence English pepo), from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn, “large melon”), from πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”), from πέπτω (péptō, “ripen”). The first attestation is from 1647. The alternative theory

parole.significato: Inflicting punishment; punishing.
parole.testo: From Middle French punitif, from Medieval Latin pūnitīvus, from pūniō (“to punish”).

parole.significato: Any small model of a person or animal able to be moved by strings or rods, or in the form of a glove.
parole.testo: From Middle English popet, probably from, though attested earlier than, Middle French poupette, diminutive of poupée (cf. also Medieval Latin *pupata), ultimately derived from Latin pupa (“doll, puppet; girl”). The nominal form first appears c. 1531, and the verbal form c. 1635. See also puppy.

parole.significato: Consisting of pus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French purulent, from Latin pūrulentus, from pūs (“pus”).

parole.significato: To apply a force to (an object) such that it moves away from the person or thing applying the force.
parole.testo: From Middle English pushen, poshen, posson, borrowed from Middle French pousser (Modern French pousser) from Old French poulser, from Latin pulsare (“to beat, strike”), frequentative of pellere (past participle pulsus). Doublet of pulsate and pulse (verb). Partly displaced native Old English sċūfan,

parole.significato: The quality or state of being pusillanimous; the vice of being timid and cowardly, and thus not living up to one's full…
parole.testo: From pusillanim(ous) + -ity, from Middle French pusillanimité, from the ecclesiastical Latin pusillanimis, from pusillus (puny) + animus (spirit) + -ous. A translation of the Greek ὀλιγόψυχος (oligópsukhos, “faint-hearted”).

parole.significato: Commonly believed or deemed to be the case; generally assumed.
parole.testo: First attested c. 1432, from Middle French putatif, from Latin putātīvus (“supposed, purported”), from putātus (“thought”), from putō (“to think, to consider, to reckon”).

parole.significato: A woman who is focused on style and leisurely pastimes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Middle English queyntrelle (“person of fashion”), from Middle French cointerelle, from Middle French cointerel (“vain”) + -elle, -ele (suffix forming feminine diminutive nouns), possibly influenced by quaint. Cointerel is derived from cointe (“clever, intelligent; quaint”), from L

parole.significato: The act or process of qualifying for a position, achievement etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French qualification in the 1540s, which in turn derives from Medieval Latin quālificātiō. By surface analysis, qual(ify) + -ification.

parole.significato: Any of the three points that divide an ordered distribution into four parts, each containing a quarter of the populatio…
parole.testo: From Middle French quartil, from Medieval Latin quartilus. By surface analysis, quart + -ile.

parole.significato: Synonym of quietness (“absence of sound”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French quiétude, from Late Latin quiētūdō, from Latin quiētus, perfect passive participle of quiēscō (“rest”).

parole.significato: An interval of one fifth.
parole.testo: * From Middle French quint, from Latin quīntus. Doublet of quintus. * (firefighting vehicle): In reference to its five functions: pump, water tank, fire hose, aerial device, and ground ladders.

parole.significato: A thing that is the most perfect example of its type; the most perfect embodiment of something; epitome, prototype.
parole.testo: PIE word  *pénkʷe From Middle English, borrowed from Middle French, from Medieval Latin quinta essentia (“fifth essence, aether”), equivalent to quint- + essence. "Essence" in this context is a synonym for "element". In pre-atomic/Aristotelian theory, there are four known elements or essences — Eart

parole.significato: having five parts or members
parole.testo: From Middle French quintuple, from Latin quīntuplus, from quīntus (“fifth”) + -plus (“-ple”).

parole.significato: A rhizome or root, especially of ginger.
parole.testo: Mid 16th century. From Middle French raïz, raiz, rais (“root”), from Latin radix (“root”), from Proto-Italic *wrādīks, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds.

parole.significato: A public gathering or mass meeting that is not mainly a protest and is organized to inspire enthusiasm for a cause.
parole.testo: From Middle French rallier (French rallier), from Old French ralier, from Latin prefix re- + ad + ligare (“to bind; to ally”).

parole.significato: A branching-out, the act or result of developing branches; specifically the divergence of the stem and limbs of a plant…
parole.testo: From Middle French ramification, or its source, Medieval Latin rāmificātiō. By surface analysis, ramify + -ication.

parole.significato: To divide into branches or subdivisions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ramifier, from Medieval Latin ramificō (“to branch, ramify”), from Latin rāmus (“a branch”) + -ficō (causative suffix).

parole.significato: The quality of being rapacious; voracity.
parole.testo: From rapac(ious) + -ity, from Middle French rapacité (whence -acity, from Latin rapācitās, from rapāx, from rapiō (“snatch, grab, carry off”).

parole.significato: To cause to experience great happiness or excitement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French rapture, from Latin raptūra, future active participle of rapiō (“snatch, carry off”).

parole.significato: A measure of the scarcity of an object.
parole.testo: From rare + -ity, borrowed from Middle French rarité, from Latin rāritās; compare French rareté. See also rare.

parole.significato: The wrist.
parole.testo: From Middle French rachette, rascette, from Late Latin racheta, rasceta (“wrist, ankle”), diminutive of rasca, from Arabic رَاحَة (rāḥa, “palm of the hand”).

parole.significato: The act or process of ratifying, or the state of being ratified.
parole.testo: From Middle French ratification, from Medieval Latin ratificatio.

parole.significato: A ray or beam of light.
parole.testo: From Middle French rayon [1539], from Old French rai (whence English ray), from Latin rādius (whence English radius).

parole.significato: To move back; to retreat; to withdraw.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English receden, from Middle French receder and its etymon Latin recedere (“to withdraw; to go back”), from re- + cedere (“to go”).

parole.significato: The act of receiving.
parole.testo: From Middle English recepcion, reception, from Middle French reception, from Latin receptiōn- (“the act of receiving; reception”), from recipiō (“receive”), from re- (“back”) + capiō (“to hold”). Equivalent to receive + -tion.

parole.significato: Synonym of recidivation (“relapse”).
parole.testo: From Middle French recidive (modern French récidive) or its etymon Latin recidīva, from the feminine of recidīvus.

parole.significato: A formula for preparing or using a medicine; a prescription; also, a medicine prepared from such instructions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French récipé, from Latin recipe, second person singular imperative of Latin recipiō (“receive”).

parole.significato: One who receives.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French récipient, from Latin recipiēns, present participle of recipiō (“to receive”).

parole.significato: The act of publicly reciting something previously memorized.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French récitation, from Latin recitatio, equivalent to recite + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of reclaiming or the state of being reclaimed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French réclamation, from Latin reclamatio. Equivalent to reclaim + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of recognizing or the condition of being recognized (matching a current observation with a memory of a prior ob…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English recognicion, from Middle French recognicion, recognition and its etymon Latin recognitiōnem (accusative of recognitiō), from recognitus, past participle of recognōscere.

parole.significato: To match (something or someone which one currently perceives) to a memory of some previous encounter with the same pers…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French reconoistre, from Old French reconoistre, from Latin recognoscere, first attested in the 16th century. Displaced native English acknow (“to recognize, perceive as”), compare German erkennen and Swedish erkänna. Latin had rare recognizare (“to try by jury”).

parole.significato: Repeat undertaking or restoration.
parole.testo: From reconduct + -ion. Borrowed from Middle French reconduction in the “repeat lease” sense, itself from Medieval Latin recondūctiō from recondūcere already used by classical Roman jurisprudence.

parole.significato: Any activity, such as play, that amuses, diverts or stimulates.
parole.testo: From Middle English recreacion, from Middle French recreacion, from Old French recreacion, from Latin recreātiō.

parole.significato: Any quadrilateral having opposing sides parallel and four right angles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin rectangulum (“right angle”), from Latin rectus (“right”) + angulus (“an angle”).

parole.significato: Straightness; the state or quality of having a constant direction and not being crooked or bent.
parole.testo: From Middle English rectitude, from Middle French rectitude, from Late Latin rectitūdō (“straightness, uprightness”), from Latin rectus (“straight”), perfect passive participle of regō (“regulate, guide”).

parole.significato: Any of certain residences for clergy members.
parole.testo: From Middle French rectorie, from Medieval Latin rectoria. See rector.

parole.significato: To disprove or refute (someone) in an argument.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English redarguen, redargue (“to defeat (someone) in an argument; to rebuke, reprove”), from Middle French redarguer and Old French redargüer (“to disprove, refute; to accuse, blame; to rebuke, reprove”) (modern French rédarguer), and from their etymon Latin redarguere (“to disprove

parole.significato: Pertaining to the reduction of a decree etc.; rescissory.
parole.testo: From Middle French réductif, from Late Latin reductivus, from the participle stem of Latin reducere (“to reduce”).

parole.significato: A relationship or relation (to something).
parole.testo: From Middle French référence, from Medieval Latin referentia, nominative neuter plural of referēns, present participle of referō (“return, reply”, literally “carry back”). Morphologically refer + -ence.

parole.significato: The act of reflecting or the state of being reflected.
parole.testo: From Middle English refleccion, refleccioun, refleccioune, reflection, from Middle French reflection, reflexion, and its source Late Latin reflexiō, from the participle stem of reflectō. The current spelling is influenced by reflect. Equivalent to reflect + -ion.

parole.significato: Dated spelling of reflection.
parole.testo: From Middle English reflexion, reflexioun, from Middle French reflexion and its etymon Late Latin reflexiō; the variant spelling reflection is due to influence from correction.

parole.significato: An improvement (or an intended improvement) in the existing form or condition of institutions or practices, etc.; inten…
parole.testo: From Middle English reformacioun, reformation, from Middle French reformation and Latin refōrmātiō, refōrmātiōnis (“reform, change”), from refōrmō (“transform, reshape”), from re- + fōrmō (“shape, form”). By surface analysis, reform + -ation.

parole.significato: An act of refuting or disproving; the disproving of an argument, opinion, testimony, doctrine or theory by argument or…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French refutation (compare French réfutation, Spanish refutación, Portuguese refutação, Italian refutazione) or its etymon Latin refūtātiō, from refūtō + -ātiō. By surface analysis, refute + -ation. First attested in 1536 (in sense 1).

parole.significato: Mode of rule or management.
parole.testo: From Middle English regime, regyme, from Middle French regime, from Latin regimen (“direction, government”). Doublet of regimen.

parole.significato: Orderly government; system of order; administration.
parole.testo: From Middle English regimen, from Middle French regimen and its etymon, Latin regimen (“guidance, direction, government, rule”). Doublet of regime.

parole.significato: A unit of armed troops under the command of an officer, and consisting of several smaller units.
parole.testo: From Middle French regement, régiment, and its source, Late Latin regimentum (“direction for government; course of medical treatment”), from Latin regō (“rule”).

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, a specific region or district.
parole.testo: From Middle French régional, from Latin regiōnālis.

parole.significato: Reigning, ruling; currently holding power.
parole.testo: From Middle English regnant, reignant, from Middle French regnant, régnant, and its source, Latin rēgnāns, the present participle of regnāre.

parole.significato: The condition or quality of being regular
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French regularite, from Old French regularite, from Late Latin rēgulāritās, rēgulāritātem, from rēgulāris; see regular. By surface analysis, regular + -ity.

parole.significato: The process of rehabilitating somebody or something.
parole.testo: From Middle French réhabilitation, from Medieval Latin rehabilitatio.

parole.significato: Connected to or depending on something else; comparative.
parole.testo: From Middle French relatif, from Late Latin relātīvus, from Latin relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (“to carry back, to ascribe”), from re- (“again”) + ferō (“to bear or carry”). By surface analysis, relate + -ive.

parole.significato: A raising or lifting up
parole.testo: From Middle English relevacion, relevacioun, relevation, from Middle French relevation and its etymon Latin relevātiō, from relevāre. See relieve. By surface analysis, relevate + -ion.
