parole.significato: Something that, or someone who, survives or remains or is left over after the loss of others; a relic.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English relicte (“widow”), from Middle French relicte (“widow”), from Late Latin relicta (“widow”), from Latin relictus, past participle of relinquō (“to abandon, to relinquish, to leave (behind)”), from re- + linquō (“to leave, quit, forsake, depart from”). Doublet of relic, d

parole.significato: To give up, abandon or retire from something; to trade away.
parole.testo: From Middle English relinquisshen, from the inflected stem relinquiss- of Middle French relinquir, from Latin relinquere, itself from re- + linquere (“to leave”). Compare also Sanskrit रिणक्ति (riṇakti, “to leave”).

parole.significato: A container to hold or display religious relics.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French reliquaire (modern French reliquaire), from Late Latin reliquiarium, from rēliquia (“a relic”) (English relic), noun use of reliquus (“abandoned, left behind, relict”), from relinquō (“to relinquish”), from re- (“again”) and linquō (“to leave”), from Proto-Indo-European *

parole.significato: The act of sending an accused person back into custody whilst awaiting trial.
parole.testo: From Middle English remaunden (“to send back”), from Middle French remander (“to send back”), from Late Latin remandare (“to send backward”), from Latin remandare (“to order”). Compare countermand.

parole.significato: An act, or the process, of renovating.
parole.testo: From Middle English renovacion, renovacyoun, from Middle French renovation and its etymon, Latin renovātiō. By surface analysis, renovate + -ion.

parole.significato: To restore to good working order, fix, or improve damaged condition; to mend; to remedy.
parole.testo: Coined between 1300 and 1350 from Middle English repairen, from Middle French reparer, from Latin reparō (“renew, repair”).

parole.significato: Able to be repaired.
parole.testo: From Middle French réparable, from Latin reparābilis.

parole.significato: A consequence or ensuing result of some action.
parole.testo: From Middle French répercussion, from Latin repercussio (“rebounding; repercussion”), from repercutio (“cause to rebound, reflect, strike against”), from re- + percutio (“beat, strike”), from per- (“thoroughly”) + quatio (“shake”).

parole.significato: Typical; having the same properties or interest as a larger group.
parole.testo: From Middle English representative, from Middle French representatif and its etymon Medieval Latin repraesentātīvus. By surface analysis, represent + -ative; See representation. Displaced native Old English spala (“a representative”).

parole.significato: A state where sovereignty rests with the people or their representatives, rather than with a monarch or emperor; a coun…
parole.testo: From Middle French republique (“republic”), from Latin rēspūblicā, from rēs (“thing”) + pūblica (“public”); hence literally “the public thing”.

parole.significato: The act of repelling or the condition of being repelled.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French répulsion, from Late Latin repulsio, repulsionem, from Latin repulsus.

parole.significato: Tending to rouse aversion or to repulse; disgusting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French repulsif, from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus. By surface analysis, repuls(e) + -ive. Compare typologically Polish odpychający (< pchnąć), Russian отта́лкивающий (ottálkivajuščij) (< толкну́ть (tolknútʹ)).

parole.significato: To rest, repose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French requiescer, from Latin requiescō; re- + quiescō (“to rest”), from quies (“rest”).

parole.significato: To start back; to recoil; to recede from a purpose.
parole.testo: From Middle French resiler (compare French résilier), from Latin resiliō (“spring back”), from re- (“back”) + saliō (“to jump”).

parole.significato: To attempt to counter the actions or effects of.
parole.testo: From Middle English resisten, from Middle French resister and Old French resistre, and their source, Latin resistere, from re- + sistere (“cause to stand”).

parole.significato: Something that one uses to achieve an objective, e.g. raw materials or personnel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ressource, from Old French resourse, resource (“a source, spring”), from resourdre, from Latin resurgō (“to rise again, spring up anew”). Equivalent to re- + source. See resourd, resurgent, source.

parole.significato: Having the duty of taking care of something; answerable for an act performed or for its consequences; accountable; amen…
parole.testo: From Middle French responsable, from Old French responsable, responsible, formed from the root of Latin responsus, from respondeō, respondēre. The spelling of the English word is taken from the Old French variant responsible. By surface analysis, response + -ible.

parole.significato: Answering, replying or responding
parole.testo: From Middle French responsif, from Late Latin responsivus.

parole.significato: Having power to retain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French rétentif, from Old French retentif, from Medieval Latin retentivus, from Latin retentus.

parole.significato: Avoidance of saying or reluctance to say too much; discretion, tight-lippedness; (countable) an instance of acting in t…
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Middle French réticence (“act of keeping silent, silence; reserve; aposiopesis”) (modern French réticence (“tight-lippedness, reticence”)), or derived from its etymon Latin reticentia (“act of keeping silent, silence; aposiopesis”), from reticēns (“keeping silent, reticent,

parole.significato: To stop working on a permanent basis, usually because of old age or illness.
parole.testo: From Middle French retirer (“draw back”), from Old French retirer, built from re- (“back”) + tirer (“draw, pull”), the latter from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre, of highly uncertain origin.

parole.significato: To cancel or take back (something, such as an edict or a favour or grant previously bestowed); to rescind, to revoke.
parole.testo: From Middle French rétracter (“to annul; to reconsider; to withdraw”) (modern French rétracter (“to retract; to contract”)), and from its etymon Latin retractāre, the present active infinitive of retractō (“to retract, withdraw; to annul, revoke; to detract from; to undertake again; to reconsider; t

parole.significato: A curtailment or reduction.
parole.testo: Probably partly from both of the following: * Middle French retrenchement, retranchement (“removal of a portion from a larger whole; reduction of expenses”) (modern French retranchement (“deduction, subtraction”)), from retrancher, retranchier (“to get rid of, remove completely; to remove a portion

parole.significato: To regain or get back something.
parole.testo: Recorded in Middle English c. 1410 as retreve (altered to retrive in the 16th century; modern form is from c. 1650), from Middle French retruev-, stem of Old French retrover (“to find again”, modern retrouver), itself from re- (“again”) + trover (“to find”), probably from Vulgar Latin *tropāre (“to

parole.significato: Directed or moving backwards in relation to the normal or previous direction of travel; retreating.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Middle English retrograd, retrograde (“of a planet: appearing to move in a direction opposite to the order of the zodiac signs, retrograde; unfortunate”), from Middle French retrograde and Old French retrograde (“of a celestial object: appearing to move backwards; movin

parole.significato: To cause (a land feature such as a coastline or waterfall) to undergo retrogradation, that is, to travel in the directi…
parole.testo: From Middle French retrograder (“to (cause to) go back, return; to (cause to) move backwards; of a celestial object: to show retrograde motion; to date to an earlier period”) (modern French rétrograder), and from its etymon Latin retrōgradī (“to go or step back or backwards; of a celestial object: t

parole.significato: The income returned by an investment.
parole.testo: Recorded in English from 1433, "income from property or possessions", from Middle French revenue, from Old French [Term?] (“a return”) (modern French revenu), the prop. feminine past participle of revenir (“come back”) (=modern French), from Latin revenire (“to return, come back”), from re- (“back”)

parole.significato: Turned up sigmoidally, with the end pointing outward; reboundant.
parole.testo: From Middle French reverberant (present participle of reverberer), or directly from Latin reverberāns (present participle of reverberō); compare French réverbérant, Italian riverberante, Portuguese reverberante, and Spanish reverberante.

parole.significato: Worthy of reverence or respect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French révérend, from Old French, from Latin future passive participle reverendus (“that is to be respected”), from deponent verb revereor (“to honor, revere”).

parole.significato: Showing or characterized by great respect or reverence; respectful.
parole.testo: From Middle English reverent, from Middle French reverent (from Old French reverent) and its etymon Latin reverēns. By surface analysis, revere + -ent.

parole.significato: To review, alter and amend, especially of written material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French réviser, from Latin revīsō, from re- + vīsō (“examine”), frequentative of videō (“see”).

parole.significato: To visit again.
parole.testo: From Middle English revisite, from Middle French revisiter and Latin revīsitāre. By surface analysis, re- + visit.

parole.significato: Having the ability of being revoked; capable of being revoked.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French révocable, from Old French revocable, from Latin revocabilis; equivalent to revoke + -able.

parole.significato: To cancel or invalidate by withdrawing or reversing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French révoquer, from Latin revocare, from re- + voco, vocare. Doublet of revocate.

parole.significato: Abhorrence, a sense of loathing, intense aversion, repugnance, repulsion, horror.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle French révulsion and partly from Latin revulsiō.

parole.significato: Resembling or relating to rheumatism.
parole.testo: From Middle French rheumatique, from Latin rheumaticus, from Ancient Greek ῥευματικός (rheumatikós), from ῥεῦμα (rheûma, “stream, flow”) from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

parole.significato: A rhombus.
parole.testo: Partly borrowed from Middle French rhombe and partly from its etymon Latin rhombus, from Ancient Greek ῥόμβος (rhómbos). Doublet of rhombus and rhumb.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to laughter.
parole.testo: From Middle French risible and directly from Late Latin rīsibilis, from Latin rīsus (“laughter”) + -ibilis, from the perfect passive participle of rīdeō (“laugh”).

parole.significato: The act of completely defeating an army or other enemy force, causing it to retreat in a disorganized manner; (by exten…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle French route (“military defeat; retreat”), from rout, archaic past participle of Middle French, Old French rompre (“to break; to break up, disperse”) (modern French rompre (“to break, snap; to break up (with someone)”)), from Latin rumpere, the present active infiniti

parole.significato: A variety of light-colored dry wine from Spain or the Canary Islands; also, any strong white wine from southern Europe;…
parole.testo: From earlier (wyne) seck from Middle French (vin (“wine”)) sec (“dry”), from Latin siccus (“dry”).

parole.significato: The plant Salvia officinalis and savory spice produced from it; also planted for ornamental purposes.
parole.testo: From Middle English sauge, from Middle French sauge, from Old French salje, from Latin salvia, from salvus (“healthy”), see safe. Doublet of salvia.

parole.significato: Salic; Salian
parole.testo: From Middle French salique, from Latin Salicus, from Salii (“Salian Franks”) + -icus.

parole.significato: A small open container holding salt for use in the kitchen or on a dining table.
parole.testo: From salt + cellar, from 15th Century Middle English saler, from Middle French salier, from Latin salārius (“relating to salt”), from Latin sāl (“salt”). Modified based on originally unrelated English cellar.

parole.significato: Effecting or designed to effect an improvement; remedial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French salutaire and its source, Latin salutaris (“healthful”), from salus (“health”).

parole.significato: That cures or restores; curative or restorative.
parole.testo: From Middle English sanatif, sanative, sanatyf, sanatyfe, sanatyve, from Middle French sanatif, from Early Medieval Latin sānātīvus, from Latin sānātus, from sānō, from sānus.

parole.significato: A hypocritical form of excessive piety, considered to be an affectation merely for public show.
parole.testo: From Middle French sanctimonie, from Latin sānctimōnia (“sanctity, sacredness; purity, chastity”), from sanctus (“holy”) + -monia (“action or result of an action”).

parole.significato: An approval, by an authority, generally one that makes something valid.
parole.testo: From Middle French sanction, from Latin sānctiō.

parole.significato: Bloody; containing blood.
parole.testo: From Middle English sanguinous, sangwynouse (“sanguine; of eyes: bloodshot”), from Middle French sanguineux and its etymon Late Latin sanguinōsus.

parole.significato: The condition of being sane.
parole.testo: From Middle English sanite, sanyte, sanytee, from Middle French sanité, from Latin sānitās, from sānus (“healthy”) + -itās (“-ity”). By surface analysis, sane + -ity.

parole.significato: A moon or other smaller body orbiting a larger one.
parole.testo: From Middle French satellite, from Latin satelles (“attendant”). Ultimately perhaps of Etruscan origin.

parole.significato: The state of being satiated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French satieté, from Latin satietas.

parole.significato: A literary device of writing or art which principally ridicules its subject often as an intended means of provoking or…
parole.testo: From Middle French satire, from Old French, from Latin satira, from earlier satura, from lanx satura (“full dish”), from feminine of satur. Altered in Latin by influence of Ancient Greek σάτυρος (sáturos, “satyr”), on the mistaken notion that the form is related to the Greek σατυρικὸν δράμα (saturik

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to satire.
parole.testo: From Middle French satirique, from Late Latin satiricus.

parole.significato: Done to satisfaction; adequate or sufficient.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French satisfactoire, from Late Latin satisfactōrius, from Latin satisfactus, past participle of satisfaciō.

parole.significato: A leap or jump, especially one made by a horse.
parole.testo: In the sense "jump (made by a horse)", from Middle French sault, saut (and in the sense "waterfall", from that word's Colonial-era descendant, 17th-century French sault, corresponding to modern French saut (“jump”)), from Latin saltus.

parole.significato: Capable of being saved.
parole.testo: From Middle English savable, from Middle French sauvable, from Old French salvable, sauvable, from Medieval Latin salvābilis; equivalent to save + -able.

parole.significato: A type of fine cloth similar to serge.
parole.testo: From Middle French saie, from Latin saga, plural of sagum (“military cloak”).

parole.significato: An incident or event that disgraces or damages the reputation of the persons or organization involved.
parole.testo: From Middle French scandale (“indignation caused by misconduct or defamatory speech”), from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum (“that on which one trips, cause of offense”, literally “stumbling block”), from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skándalon, “a trap laid for an enemy, a cause of moral stumbling”), fro

parole.significato: scapular
parole.testo: From Middle French scapulaire and Latin scapulārius. By surface analysis, scapula + -ary.

parole.significato: A beetle of the species Scarabaeus sacer, sacred to the ancient Egyptians.
parole.testo: From Middle French scarabée, from Latin scarabaeus (“beetle”). Doublet of scarabaeus, now obsolete.

parole.significato: The location of an event that attracts attention.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English scene, from Middle French scene, borrowed from Latin sc(a)ena, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ, “scene, stage”). Doublet of scena and skene.

parole.significato: having beautiful scenery; picturesque
parole.testo: From Middle French scénique, from Latin scēnicus, alternative form of scaenicus (“of or pertaining to the stage; theatrical, scenic”), from Ancient Greek σκηνικός (skēnikós, “theatrical”), from σκηνή (skēnḗ, “stage”).

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English cedule, from Middle French cedule (whence French cédule), from Old French cedule, from Late Latin schedula (“papyrus strip”), diminutive of Latin scheda, from Ancient Greek σχέδη (skhédē, “papyrus leaf”), from Proto-Hellenic *skʰíd͏̌d͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *skid-

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a schism.
parole.testo: From Middle English scismatik with etymological respelling, from Middle French scismatique, from Latin schismaticus, from Ancient Greek σχισματικός (skhismatikós), from σχίσμα (skhísma, “cleft, division”). The music sense is based on schisma, from the same ultimate Greek source; compare schism.

parole.significato: A member of the medieval philosophical school of scholasticism; a medieval Christian Aristotelian.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French scholastique, from Latin scholasticus, from Ancient Greek σχολαστικός (skholastikós).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the ischium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French sciatique, from Late Latin sciaticus, variant of ischiadicus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”).

parole.significato: Related or connected to science
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French scientifique, from Medieval Latin scientificus (“pertaining to science”).

parole.significato: Exactly and carefully conducted.
parole.testo: From Middle French scrupuleux, from Latin scrupulosus.

parole.significato: In a careful manner, with scruple; done with careful attention to detail.
parole.testo: From scrupulous + -ly, from Middle French scrupuleux, from Latin scrūpulōsus (“careful, scrupulous”), from scrūpulus (“anxiety, uneasiness”), diminutive from scrūpus (“sharp stone; anxiety”) + -ulus.

parole.significato: To transfer temporarily to alternative employment.
parole.testo: From Middle French seconder, from Latin secundō (“assist, make favorable”).

parole.significato: The condition of not being threatened, especially physically, psychologically, emotionally, or financially.
parole.testo: From secure + -ity, from Middle English securite, from Middle French securité (modern sécurité), from Latin sēcūritās, from Latin sēcūrus (“safe, secure”), from sē- (“without”) + cūra (“care”); see cure. Similar to Latin sine cūrā (“without care, carefree”), which led to English sinecure. Doublet of

parole.significato: Not moving; relatively still; staying in the vicinity.
parole.testo: From Middle French sédentaire, from Latin sedentārius (“sitting”), from sedeō (“to sit, to be seated”).

parole.significato: A collection of small particles, particularly dirt, that precipitates from a river or other body of water.
parole.testo: From Middle French sédiment, from Latin sedimentum < sedeō.

parole.significato: Of, related to, or being involved in sedition.
parole.testo: From Middle French séditieux, from Latin seditiosus.

parole.significato: The act of seducing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French séduction, from Latin sēductiō, from sēdūcō. Equivalent to seduce + -tion.

parole.significato: One who seduces.
parole.testo: From Middle English seductor, seductour, from Middle French seducteur, from Latin sēductor.

parole.significato: Emotions or feelings arising from or relating to aesthetic or moral standards, especially those which are sensitive and…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English sensibilite (“physical ability to sense or perceive; sensitivity to pain; type of perception by a sense organ; perception, understanding; image imprinted on the mind during perception; (philosophy) capacity of the soul to receive information from the senses, perceptibility;

parole.significato: Having the faculty of sensation; pertaining to the senses.
parole.testo: From Middle French sensitif, from Medieval Latin sensitivus. By surface analysis, sense + -ite + -ive.

parole.significato: The state of being sensual or sensuous.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French sensualité, derived from Late Latin sēnsuālitātem (“sensibility, capacity for sensation”). By surface analysis, sensual + -ity.

parole.significato: The decision or judgement of a jury or court; a verdict.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French sentence, from Latin sententia (“way of thinking, opinion, sentiment”), from sentiēns, present participle of sentiō (“to feel, think”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”).

parole.significato: Able to be separated.
parole.testo: From Middle English separable, from Middle French separable and its etymon Latin sēparābilis.

parole.significato: The events, collectively, which follow a previously mentioned event; the aftermath.
parole.testo: From Middle English sequele, sequelle, sequile, from Middle French sequele, sequelle and its etymon, Latin sequēla, from sequī (“to follow”). Doublet of sequela.

parole.significato: That comes after in time or order; subsequent.
parole.testo: 1550s; borrowed from Middle French sequent, from Old French sequent, itself borrowed from Latin sequentem, present participle of sequī (“to follow”).

parole.significato: The process or act of sequestering; a putting aside or separating.
parole.testo: From Middle French sequestration, from Late Latin sequestrātiō, from Latin sequestrō (“sequester”).

parole.significato: A fine rain from a cloudless sky after sunset.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French serein, from Old French serein (“evening”), from Vulgar Latin *serānum, from substantive use of sērum, neuter of sērus (“late”) + -ānus suffix.

parole.significato: The state of being a slave; slavery; being forced to work for others or do their bidding without one's consent or again…
parole.testo: From Middle French servitude, from Latin servitūdō, from Latin servus (“slave”). Equivalent to serve + -itude.

parole.significato: Synonym of sestertius.
parole.testo: From Middle French sesterce, from Latin sēstertius (“two-and-a-half (asses)”).

parole.significato: Very bad or intense.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Latin severus (“severe, serious, grave in demeanor”).

parole.significato: The state of being severe.
parole.testo: From Middle English severity, from Middle French severite (modern French sévérité), from Latin sevēritās. By surface analysis, severe + -ity.

parole.significato: The extent to which something matters; importance
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English significaunce, from Middle French significance, from Old French significance, from Latin significantia. Doublet of signifiance.

parole.significato: Something that simulates a system or environment in order to predict actual behaviour.
parole.testo: First attested in 1340 as Middle English symulacioun, from Middle French simulation, from Old French simulation/simulacion, from Latin simulātiōnem, from simulō (“imitate”). Morphologically simulate + -ion.

parole.significato: Genuine, honest, and free from pretense or deceit; heartfelt.
parole.testo: From Middle French sincere, from Latin sincerus (“genuine”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together”) (whence English sam) + *ḱer- (“grow”) (whence Latin Ceres, the goddess of harvest, etymon of cereal). Not from sine (“without”) + cera (“wax”), which is a folk etymology; see Wikipedia page.

parole.significato: A bent pipe or tube with one end lower than the other, in which hydrostatic pressure exerted due to the force of gravit…
parole.testo: From Middle French siphon, from Old French sifon, from Latin sīphō, from Ancient Greek σίφων (síphōn, “pipe, tube”), of uncertain origin; possibly related to Latin tibia (“pipe, flute of bone”), with the irregular forms suggesting a non-Indo-European loan source, perhaps of the shape *twi-, *twibh.

parole.significato: The combination of circumstances at a given moment; a state of affairs.
parole.testo: From Middle English situacioun, situacion, from Middle French situation, from Medieval Latin situatio (“position, situation”), from situare (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”). By surface analysis, situate + -ion.

parole.significato: A lizard of the family Scincidae, having small or reduced limbs or none at all and long tails that are regenerated when…
parole.testo: From Middle French scinc, from Latin scincus, from Ancient Greek σκίγγος (skíngos), σκίγκος (skínkos).

parole.significato: The skill, tendency or property of being sociable or social, of interacting well with others.
parole.testo: From Middle French sociabilité, from Latin sociābilis.

parole.significato: Tending to socialize or be social.
parole.testo: From Middle French sociable, from Latin sociābilis.

parole.significato: Being extroverted or outgoing.
parole.testo: From Middle French social, from Latin sociālis (“of or belonging to a companion or companionship or association, social”), from socius (“a companion, fellow, partner, associate, ally”), from sequor (“follow”). Cognate with English seg (“man, companion, fellow”). More at seg.

parole.significato: A long-standing group of people sharing cultural aspects such as language, dress, norms of behavior and artistic forms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French societé, from Old French societé, from Latin societās, societātem (“fellowship, association, alliance, union, community”), from socius (“associated, allied; partner, companion, ally”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-yo- (“companion”), from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to

parole.significato: An error or improper usage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French solecisme, soloëcisme (French solécisme) or its etymon Latin soloecismus, from Ancient Greek σολοικισμός (soloikismós), from σόλοικος (sóloikos, “speaking incorrectly”), from Σόλοι (Sóloi), an ancient Athenian colony in Cilicia whose inhabitants spoke a dialect regarded b

parole.significato: the action or instance of soliciting; petition; proposal
parole.testo: From Middle French sollicitation, from Latin sollicitātiō.

parole.significato: A substance in the fundamental state of matter that retains its size and shape without need of a container (as opposed…
parole.testo: From Middle English solid, from the adjective, Middle French solide, or Latin solidum. Doublet of solidum.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being solid.
parole.testo: From solid + -ity, from Middle French solidité, from Latin soliditās.

parole.significato: A state of drowsiness or sleepiness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French somnolence, from Late Latin somnolentia, derived from Latin somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos (“sleep, slumber”).

parole.significato: The service tree, Sorbus domestica.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French sorbier (the tree), sorbe (the fruit), from Latin sorbus (the tree), sorbum (the fruit). See service tree.

parole.significato: Magical power; the use of witchcraft or magic arts.
parole.testo: From Middle English sorcery, borrowed from Middle French sorcerie, ultimately derived from Latin sors (“fate”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”). Cognate with serō, seriēs, sermō. Compare also French sorcier.

parole.significato: To sprinkle or spray.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French espargier, from Latin spargō (whence English sparse), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pregʰ- (“to scatter, to jerk”).

parole.significato: An explicit set of requirements to be satisfied by a material, product, or service.
parole.testo: From Middle French specification, from Medieval Latin specificationem (accusative of specificatio).

parole.significato: A ghostly apparition, a phantom.
parole.testo: From Middle French spectre, from Latin spectrum (“appearance, apparition”). Doublet of spectrum.

parole.significato: A buttery or pantry.
parole.testo: From Middle English spence, spense, borrowed from Middle French despense, from Medieval Latin dīspēnsa, noun use of feminine of Latin dīspēnsus, past participle of dīspendere (“weigh out”).

parole.significato: A pin or peg used to stop the vent in a cask.
parole.testo: From Middle English spigot (“wooden stopper”). Probably ultimately from Latin spīca via Old Occitan espiga and Middle French espigeot.

parole.significato: A small copse or wood, especially one planted as a shelter for game birds.
parole.testo: From Middle English spenné, from Middle French espinoye (“thorny thicket”), espinaye, from Latin spīnētum (“thorny thicket”), from Latin spīna (“thorn”).

parole.significato: A curve that is the locus of a point that rotates about a fixed point while continuously increasing its distance from t…
parole.testo: From Middle French spirale, from Medieval Latin spiralis, from Latin spīra, from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra, “wreath, coil, twist”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being spiritual.
parole.testo: From Middle French spiritualité, from Late Latin spīrituālitās.

parole.significato: To weaken, as a joint, ligament, or muscle, by sudden and excessive exertion, as by wrenching; to overstrain, or stretc…
parole.testo: Origin unknown. Noun attested since 1601; verb attested 1622. Possibly borrowed from Middle French espraindre (“to squeeze or press out”), from Latin exprimere (“to squeeze out, express”), in which case cognate to express.

parole.significato: To transform from an earthly body into a celestial body; to place in the sky as such
parole.testo: From Middle English stellifien (“to make into a star; glorify, deify”), from Middle French stellifier, from Medieval Latin stellificāre, itself from Latin stella (“star”) + faciō (“make, do”).

parole.significato: A thin sheet, either perforated or using some other technique, with which a pattern may be produced upon a surface; a u…
parole.testo: Likely a nominalization of Middle English stencellen (“to garnish with bright hues”), borrowed from Middle French estinceller (“to glisten”), from Old French estenceler (“to spark”), from Old French estencele (“spark”), from Vulgar Latin *stincilla, from metathesis of Latin scintilla (“spark”). The

parole.significato: Unable to reproduce (or procreate).
parole.testo: From Middle French stérile, from Latin sterilis (“barren, futile”). See also Ancient Greek στεῖρα (steîra).

parole.significato: Having or revealing little emotion or sensibility.
parole.testo: From Middle French stolide, from Latin stolidus (“foolish, obtuse, slow”).

parole.significato: The property of being stolid; unemotionality.
parole.testo: From stolid + -ity, from Middle French stolidité, from Late Latin stoliditas.

parole.significato: A cohesive whole built up of distinct parts.
parole.testo: From Middle French structure, from Latin structūra (“a fitting together, adjustment, building, erection, a building, edifice, structure”), from struere, past participle structus (“pile up, arrange, assemble, build”). Compare construct, instruct, destroy, etc.

parole.significato: The state of extreme shock or astonishment.
parole.testo: From Middle French stupéfaction, from Latin stupefaciō (“strike dumb, stun with amazement, stupefy”), from stupeō (“to be stunned, speechless”) (English stupid, stupor) + faciō (“to do, make”).

parole.significato: To dull the senses or capacity to think thereby reducing responsiveness; to stun.
parole.testo: From Middle French stupéfier, from Latin stupefaciō (“strike dumb, stun with amazement, stupefy”), from stupeō (“to be stunned, speechless”) (see English stupid, stupor) + faciō (“to do, make”).

parole.significato: Without intelligence.
parole.testo: From Middle French stupide, from Latin stupidus (“struck senseless, amazed”), from stupeō (“be amazed or confounded, be struck senseless”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tup-, *(s)tewp- (“to push, stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”). Cognate with Old High German stubarōn (“to

parole.significato: The quality of being sweet or pleasing to the mind; agreeableness; pleasantness
parole.testo: From Middle English suavite, suavitee, suavyte, from Middle French suavité and its etymon Latin suāvitās.

parole.significato: Of a lower rank or position; inferior or secondary; especially (military) ranking as a junior officer, below the rank o…
parole.testo: From Middle French subalterne, from Late Latin subalternus, from Latin sub- + alternus, from alter.

parole.significato: Used for sublimation.
parole.testo: From Middle French sublimatoire, from Medieval Latin sublīmātōrius.

parole.significato: Synonym of sublimate.
parole.testo: PIE word  *upó Partly from the following: * From Middle English sublimen, sublime, sublyme (“to exalt, extol, glorify, honour; (alchemy) to refine (a substance) by vaporizing in a closed container; to obtain (a substance) by cooling vapour obtained through sublimation; to extract (a pure substance)

parole.significato: High, tall, towering; also, positioned in a high place; high-up, lofty.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Middle French sublime (“admirable, excellent, perfect; placed in a high position; reaching a great height; of a person: of high office or rank”) (modern French sublime), and from its etymon Latin sublīmis, sublīmus (“elevated, raised; exalted, uplifted, sublime”, adject

parole.significato: The quality or state of being sublime.
parole.testo: From Middle English sublimite, sublimitee, from Middle French sublimité and/or Latin sublīmitās. By surface analysis, sublime + -ity.

parole.significato: The process of making or classing (something or somebody) as subordinate.
parole.testo: From Middle French subordination, from Medieval Latin subordinatio.

parole.significato: Following in time; coming or being after something else at any time, indefinitely.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French subséquent, from Latin subsequentis, form of subsequēns, present participle of subsequor (“to follow, to succeed”).

parole.significato: Auxiliary or supplemental.
parole.testo: From Middle French subsidiaire, from Latin subsidiarius (“belonging to a reserve”).

parole.significato: Real being; existence.
parole.testo: From Middle English subsistence; partly from Middle French subsistence (modern French subsistance) and partly from its etymon Late Latin subsistentia (“substance, reality, in Medieval Latin also stability”), from Latin subsistēns, present participle of subsistere (“to continue, subsist”). Perhaps al

parole.significato: The act of substituting or the state of being substituted.
parole.testo: From Middle French substitution, from Late Latin substitutio.

parole.significato: An indirect or deceptive device or stratagem; a blind. Refers especially to war and diplomatics.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French subterfuge m, from Medieval Latin subterfugium n, from Latin subterfugiō (“to flee secretly”), from subter (“under”) and fugiō (“to flee”).

parole.significato: Cunning, craftiness.
parole.testo: From subtile + -ity, from Middle French subtilité, from Latin subtīlitas. See subtle. Doublet of subtlety.

parole.significato: A subsidy; provision of financial or other support.
parole.testo: From Middle French subvention, from Late Latin subventio, from Latin subvenio (assist).

parole.significato: To be enough or sufficient; to meet the need (of anything); to be adequate; to be good enough.
parole.testo: From Middle English suffisen, from Middle French souffire, from Latin sufficiō (“supply, be adequate”), from sub (“under”) + faciō (“do, make”). Cognate with French suffire.

parole.significato: Asphyxia—a condition in which an extreme decrease in the concentration of oxygen in the body accompanied by an increase…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English suffocation, suffocacioun, from Middle French suffocation, from Latin suffocatio.

parole.significato: The right or chance to vote, express an opinion, or participate in a decision, especially in a democratic election.
parole.testo: From Middle English suffrage (“prayers or pleas on behalf of another”), from Middle French suffrage (from Old French suffrage) and its etymon Classical Latin suffrāgium (“support, vote, right of voting”). Not related to suffer. The sense of "vote" or "right to vote" was directly derived from Classic

parole.significato: Extremely costly; suggesting great expense.
parole.testo: From Middle French sumptueux, from Latin sumptuōsus, from sūmptus (“cost, charge, expense”), from sumō (“to take”) + -tus (noun formation suffix).

parole.significato: Variant spelling of supersede.
parole.testo: From Middle English superceden, from Middle French superceder, from Latin supersedēre: super- (“over-”) + sedēre (“to sit”).

parole.significato: Superior to or notable above all others; outstanding; supremely remarkable.
parole.testo: From Middle French supereminent, and its source, Late Latin supereminens, adjectival use of Latin superēminēre (corresponding to super- + eminent).

parole.significato: Above nature; beyond or added to nature, often so considered because it is given by a deity or some force beyond that w…
parole.testo: From Middle English supernatural, supernaturel, from Middle French supernaturel, from Latin supernātūrālis, from super (“above”) + nātūra (“nature; that which we are born with”), from nātus (“born”), perfect passive participle of nāscī (“to be born”) + adjective suffix -ālis. By surface analysis, su

parole.significato: A type of lettering form that appears as a number, figure, or symbol above the normal line of type, located at the righ…
parole.testo: From Middle French superscript, from Latin superscriptus (“written above”). By surface analysis, super- + script.

parole.significato: Something written (or engraved) on the surface, outside, or above something else; specifically, an address on a letter,…
parole.testo: From Middle French superscription, or its source, Late Latin superscriptio, from superscribere.

parole.significato: To take the place of.
parole.testo: From Middle French superseder (“postpone, defer”), from Latin supersedēre, from super (“over”) + sedēre (“to sit”). The meaning “to replace” is from 1642, probably by association with unrelated precede – note that c instead of s (from cēdere (“to yield”), not sedēre (“to sit”)). As a result, superce

parole.significato: A belief considered to be irrational, unfounded, or based solely on fear and ignorance, particularly credulous reverenc…
parole.testo: From Middle French superstition, from Latin superstitio (“superstition”), from superstāre (“to stand above, to stand upon, to survive”) + -tiō (“-tion: forming nouns”), from super- (“above, over, upon”) + stāre (“to stand”).

parole.significato: To suppress (in various senses).
parole.testo: From Middle English supprymen, from Middle French supprimer and its etymon Latin supprimere, supprimō (“to press down, suppress”), from sub- (“under, down”) + premō (“to press”).

parole.significato: Dominant, having power over all others.
parole.testo: From Middle English suppreme, partly from Middle French suppreme, supreme and partly from its etymon, Latin suprēmus, superlative of superus (“that is above”). In the cooking sense, partly an independent borrowing of French suprême, partly merged with the existing English word. Doublet of supremo.

parole.significato: Physically secure and certain, non-failing, reliable.
parole.testo: From Middle English sure, seur, sur, from Middle French sur or Old French seür, from Latin sēcūrus (“secure”, literally “carefree”), from sē- (“apart”) + cūra (“care”) (compare Old English orsorg (“carefree”), from or- (“without”) + sorg (“care”)). See cure. Doublet of secure and the now obsolete or

parole.significato: Of, relating to, used in, or resulting from surgery.
parole.testo: From Middle English cirurgical, borrowed from Middle French cirurgical, from Medieval Latin cirurgicālis, ultimately from Ancient Greek χειρουργία (kheirourgía), from χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). Replaced Old English Old English læċe (“doctor, physician”). By surface analysis, surge

parole.significato: Something unexpected.
parole.testo: From Middle English surprise, borrowed from Middle French surprise (“an overtake”), nominal use of the past participle of Old French sorprendre (“to overtake”), from sor- (“over”) + prendre (“to take”), from Latin super- + Latin prendere, contracted from prehendere (“to grasp, seize”). Doublet of su

parole.significato: To encircle something or simultaneously extend in all directions.
parole.testo: From Middle English sourrounden (“to submerge, overflow”), from Middle French souronder, suronder, from Late Latin superundō, from super + undō (“to rise in waves”), from unda (“wave”).

parole.significato: A tool, used by blacksmiths and other metalworkers, for shaping of a metal item.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English swage, from Middle French souage, from Old French souage (“decorative groove”), from soue (“rope”), from Vulgar Latin *soca, from Gaulish *souca (“cord”), from Proto-Celtic *soukā, from Proto-Indo-European *sew- (“to twist, bend”).

parole.significato: A feeling of pity or sorrow for the suffering or distress of another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French sympathie, from Late Latin sympathīa (“feeling in common”), from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sŭmpắtheiă, “fellow feeling”), from σῠμπᾰθής (sŭmpăthḗs, “affected by like feelings; exerting mutual influence, interacting”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, “-y”, nominal suffix). Equivalent to sym- (

parole.significato: A device used for injecting or drawing fluids through a membrane.
parole.testo: From Middle French syringe (“syringe”), from Latin sȳringem, accusative of sȳrinx (“reed, panpipe”), from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pipe, syrinx”). Doublet of syrinx.

parole.significato: A group or set of related things that operate together as a complex whole.
parole.testo: Partly borrowed from Middle French sisteme, systeme, partly directly from its etymon Late Latin systēma (“harmony; musical scale; set of celestial objects; set of troops; system”), from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “musical scale; organized body; whole made of several parts or members”), from σῠν

parole.significato: Tangible; perceptible to the sense of touch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tactile, from Latin tactilis (“that may be touched, tangible”), from tangere (“to touch”).

parole.significato: A contamination, decay or putrefaction, especially in food.
parole.testo: From Middle French teint, from Old French teint (past participle of teindre (“to dye, to tinge”)), from Latin tinctum (past participle of tingere); compare tint.

parole.significato: Retaliation; retribution.
parole.testo: From Middle French talion, from Latin talis (“such”).

parole.significato: Touchable; able to be touched or felt; perceptible by the sense of touch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tangible, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tangere (“to touch”)

parole.significato: A perennial herb, the wormwood species Artemisia dracunculus, from Europe and parts of Asia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French targon (cf. modern estragon), from Medieval Latin tragonia, from Arabic طَرْخُون (ṭarḵūn), ultimately from Ancient Greek δρακόντιον (drakóntion, “dragonwort, Dracunculus vulgaris”), from δράκων (drákōn, “dragon, serpent”). Doublet of estragon.

parole.significato: Money or goods collected by a government (or an entity to whom the government has delegated this power, e.g. in tax far…
parole.testo: From Middle English taxe, from Middle French taxe, from Medieval Latin taxa, from Latin taxō (“to appraise, value, estimate; (medieval) to tax”). Doublet of task. Displaced native Old English gafol, which was also the word for “tribute” and “rent”.

parole.significato: A person's usual manner of thinking, behaving or reacting.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English temperament, borrowed from Middle French tempérament, from Latin temperāmentum.

parole.significato: Of or situated in the temples of the head or the sides of the skull behind the orbits.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French timporal, temporal, from Late Latin temporālis, from tempora (“the temples of the head”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of temporalis.

parole.significato: To deliberately act evasively or prolong a discussion in order to gain time or postpone a decision, sometimes so that a…
parole.testo: From Middle French temporiser (“to wait one's time, temporize”) + English -ize (suffix forming verbs). parole.significato: The quality or state of being tenacious, or persistence of purpose; tenaciousness.
parole.testo: From Middle French ténacité, from Latin tenācitās (whence -acity).

parole.significato: To make a tender of; to offer or tender.
parole.testo: From Middle English tenden, from Middle French tendre, from Old French tendre (“to stretch, stretch out, hold forth, offer, tender”), from Latin tendere (“to stretch, stretch out, extend, spread out”).

parole.significato: A thin, spirally coiling stem that attaches a plant to its support.
parole.testo: From Middle French tendrillon (“bud, shoot, cartilage”), perhaps a diminutive of tendron (“cartilage”), from Old French tendre (“soft”) (see tender (adjective)), or else from Latin tendere (“to stretch, extend”) (see tender (verb)).

parole.significato: The condition of being held in a state between two or more forces, which are acting in opposition to each other.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tension, from Latin tēnsiō.

parole.significato: A roll of lint or linen, or a conical or cylindrical piece of sponge or other absorbent, used chiefly to dilate a natur…
parole.testo: From Middle English tente (“a probe”), from Middle French tente, deverbal of tenter, from Latin tentāre (“to probe, test”), alteration of temptāre (“to test, probe, tempt”).

parole.significato: To settle, determine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French terminer, from Latin termināre. Doublet of terminate.

parole.significato: The quality of being terrible.
parole.testo: From Middle English terryblete, from Middle French terribleté, terribilité and its etymon, Late Latin terribilitās.

parole.significato: A dog from a group of small, lively breeds, originally bred for the hunting of burrowing prey such as rats, rabbits, fo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French chien terrier (“terrier dog”), from chien (“dog”) + Old French terrier (“of earth”, adjective), from Medieval Latin terrarius (“of earth”), from Latin terra (“earth”).

parole.significato: To frighten greatly; to fill with terror.
parole.testo: From Middle French terrifier, from Latin terrificare.

parole.significato: Intense dread, fright, or fear.
parole.testo: From late Middle English terrour, from Old French terreur f (“terror, fear, dread”), from Latin terror (“fright, fear, terror”), from terrēre (“to frighten, terrify”), from Old Latin tr̥reō, from Proto-Italic *trozeō, from Proto-Indo-European *tre- (“to shake”), *tres- (“to tremble”).

parole.significato: The feel or shape of a surface or substance; the smoothness, roughness, softness, etc. of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French texture, borrowed from Latin textūra (“a weaving, web, texture, structure”), from textus, past participle of texere (“to weave”). See text. Doublet of tessitura.

parole.significato: The study of God, a god, or gods; and of the truthfulness of religion in general.
parole.testo: From Middle English theologie, from Middle French theologie, from Old French theologie, from Latin theologia, from Koine Greek θεολογία (theología), from θεολόγος (theológos, adjective), from θεός (theós) + λόγος (lógos). By surface analysis, theo- + -logy.

parole.significato: A mathematical statement of some importance that has been proven to be true. Minor theorems are often called propositio…
parole.testo: From Middle French théorème, from Late Latin theōrēma, from Ancient Greek θεώρημα (theṓrēma, “speculation, proposition to be proved”) (Euclid), from θεωρέω (theōréō, “to look at, view, consider, examine”), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”), from θέα (théa, “a view”) + ὁράω (horáō, “to see, look”).

parole.significato: A description of an event or system that is considered to be accurate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French théorie, a learned borrowing from Late Latin theōria, borrowed from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).

parole.significato: The act, or an instance, of burning incense.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French thurification, from Late Latin thurificatio, from Latin thurificatus; equivalent to thus (“incense”) + -ification.

parole.significato: A type of inflorescence; a compact panicle having an obscured main axis and cymose subaxes.
parole.testo: From Middle French thyrse, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Doublet of thyrsus, torse, and torso.

parole.significato: Lacking in courage or confidence.
parole.testo: From Middle French timide, from Latin timidus (“full of fear, fearful, timid”), from timeō (“to fear”).

parole.significato: The state of being timid; shyness.
parole.testo: From timid + -ity, from Middle French timidité, from Latin timiditātem.

parole.significato: A form of government in which ambition for honor, power and military glory motivates the rulers.
parole.testo: 1580s, from Middle French tymocracie, from Medieval Latin (13th century) timocratia, from Ancient Greek τῑμοκρατίᾱ (tīmokratíā), from τῑμή (tīmḗ, “valuation; honor”) + -κρατίᾱ (-kratíā, “a rule, reign”), from κρατέω (kratéō, “to rule”) (see -cracy).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, being, derived from, or having a title.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French titulaire, from Latin titulāris, from titulus (“title”).

parole.significato: A toga.
parole.testo: From Middle English toge, from Middle French toge and Latin toga. Doublet of toga and tog.

parole.significato: Capable of being borne, tolerated or endured; bearable or endurable.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English tolerable, borrowed from Middle French tolerable, from Latin tolerābilis.

parole.significato: Endurance of evil, suffering etc.
parole.testo: From Middle French toleration, from Latin tolerātiōnem, accusative singular of tolerātiō, from the verb tolerō (“to tolerate”). Compare tolerance.

parole.significato: One in a series of volumes.
parole.testo: From Middle French tome, from Latin tomus (“section of larger work”), from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos, “section, roll of papyrus, volume”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, separate”).

parole.significato: A twist of cloth or wreath, typically placed underneath and forming part of a crest (as an orle or wreath) and customar…
parole.testo: From Middle French torse (“wreath”), from Latin torqueō (“to twist”). Doublet of trousse and truss.

parole.significato: The act of turning or twisting, or the state of being twisted; the twisting or wrenching of a body by the exertion of a…
parole.testo: From Middle English torcion, from Middle French torsion, from Late Latin torsiōnem, from Latin tortiō, from torqueō (“twist, turn”). See torture, -tort.

parole.significato: An identifying characteristic, habit or trend.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French trait (“line, feature”), from Latin tractus (“drawing, pulling”), from Latin trahō. Doublet of tract.

parole.significato: Free from emotional or mental disturbance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tranquille, from Latin tranquillus, from trāns- + the root of quiēs (“rest, quiet, peace”), ultimately from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”).

parole.significato: The act of conducting or carrying out (business, negotiations, plans).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French transaction, from Old French transaccion, from Late Latin transactio. By surface analysis, trans- + action.

parole.significato: The act or process of transcribing, or converting spoken (or sometimes signed) language to the written form.
parole.testo: From Middle French transcription, or directly from Latin transcriptiōnem, from trānscrībō (“transcribe”).

parole.significato: To render motionless, by arousing terror, amazement or awe.
parole.testo: From Middle French transfixer, from Old French transfixer, from Latin transfigō (“to pierce through”), from trans- (“through”) + figō (“to pierce”).

parole.significato: To change greatly the appearance or form of.
parole.testo: From Middle English transformen, from Old French transformer, from Latin transformo, transformare, from trans (“across”, preposition) + forma (“form”).

parole.significato: The act of transforming or the state of being transformed.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English transformacioun, from Middle French, from Ecclesiastical Latin trānsfōrmātiō. Morphologically transform + -ation.

parole.significato: The process of change from one form, state, style or place to another.
parole.testo: From Middle French transition, from Latin transitio. By surface analysis, transit + -ion.

parole.significato: Lasting only a short time; temporary.
parole.testo: From Middle French transitoire, from Old French, from Latin trānsitōrius.

parole.significato: To transmute, change.
parole.testo: From Middle French transmuer, from Latin transmūtāre.

parole.significato: The loss of water by evaporation in terrestrial plants, especially through the stomata; accompanied by a corresponding…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French transpiration, from Medieval Latin transpiratio, from transpiro, from Latin trans + spiro.

parole.significato: To give off (vapour, waste matter etc.); to exhale (an odour etc.).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French transpirer, from Medieval Latin transpirare (“to breathe through”), from Latin trans (“across”) spirare (“to breathe”). The sense “to become known” is also present in French, while the sense “to happen” is not; the latter probably developed in English from the former.

parole.significato: The act or process of transposing or interchanging.
parole.testo: From Middle French transposition, from Medieval Latin transpositio.

parole.significato: Running or lying across; transverse.
parole.testo: From Middle French transversal, from Medieval Latin trānsversālis, from Latin trānsversus.

parole.significato: A crossbeam.
parole.testo: From Middle English trave, from Middle French trave, from Latin trabem, accusative of trabs (“beam, thing made using beams”).

parole.significato: A grandfather's grandfather; a great-great-grandfather.
parole.testo: From Middle French trisayeul, from Latin tris, tres (“three”) + French aïeul (“grandfather”). Compare besaiel, and see ayle.

parole.significato: A woman who engages in sexual activity with another woman; a lesbian.
parole.testo: From Middle French tribade, and its source, Latin tribad-, from Koine Greek τριβάς (tribás), from Ancient Greek τρίβω (tríbō, “to rub”).

parole.significato: To pay as tribute.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Middle English tribut (14th c.), from Middle French tribut, from Latin tributum (“tribute”, literally “a thing contributed or paid”), past participle of tribuere (“to assign, allot”), usually derived from tribus (“tribe”, which see).

parole.significato: Triple; threefold.
parole.testo: From Middle English trine, from Middle French trin, from Latin trīnus.

parole.significato: An object, usually in the form of a statuette, cup, or shield, awarded for success in a competition or to mark a specia…
parole.testo: From Middle French trophée, from Latin trophaeum (“a sign of victory, a monument”), tropaeum, from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion, “monument of an enemy's defeat”), from neuter of τροπαῖος (tropaîos, “of defeat”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “a rout, a turning of an enemy”). Doublet of tropæum.

parole.significato: A mason’s tool, used in spreading and dressing mortar, and breaking bricks to shape them.
parole.testo: From Middle English trowell, trouel, truel, from Middle French truelle, from Late Latin truella, from Classical Latin trulla, the diminutive of trua (“ladle”). Doublet of trullo.

parole.significato: Cruel or savage.
parole.testo: First attested circa 1540, from Middle French, from Latin truculentus (“fierce, savage”), from trux (“fierce, wild”).

parole.significato: To supply with, or enclose in, a tube.
parole.testo: From Middle French tube, from Latin tubus (“tube, pipe”), related to tuba (“long trumpet; war-trumpet”), of obscure ultimate origin, but possibly connected to tībia (“shinbone, reed-pipe”); see there. Doublet of tubus.

parole.significato: To turn (a laminar flow) into a turbulent flow.
parole.testo: From turbul(ent) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Middle English turbulent, from Middle French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus, from turba (“disorder, tumult, crowd”).

parole.significato: Violently disturbed or agitated; tempestuous, tumultuous.
parole.testo: From Middle English turbulent, from Middle French turbulent, from Latin turbulentus, from turba (“disorder, tumult, crowd”).

parole.significato: Inherent baseness, depravity or wickedness; corruptness and evilness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French turpitude, from Latin turpitūdō (“baseness, infamy”), from turpis (“foul, base”).

parole.significato: Fertile growth, abundance, fruitfulness; copiousness, plenty.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English uberte, from Middle French uberté, from Latin ūbertās, from ūber (“womb”).

parole.significato: Promoting the supremacy of the Pope.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ultramontain, from Late Latin ultramontanus.

parole.significato: Of a reddish brown colour, like that of the pigment.
parole.testo: From Middle French ombre (“umber”), from terre d'ombre (“dark ochre”), from Old French umbre (“shade, shadow”), from Latin umbra. Doublet of umbra.

parole.significato: A feeling of anger or annoyance caused by something offensive.
parole.testo: From Middle French ombrage (“umbrage”), from Old French ombrage, from Latin umbrāticus (“in the shade”), from umbra (“shadow, shade”).

parole.significato: The condition of agreement by all parties, the state of being unanimous.
parole.testo: From unanim(ous) + -ity, from Middle French unanimité, from Late Latin ūnanimitās. Displaced native Old English ānmōdnes (literally “one-mindedness”).

parole.significato: Unvarying; all the same.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French uniforme, from Latin uniformis.

parole.significato: Cause to become one; make into a unit; consolidate; merge; combine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French unifier, from Late Latin unificare.

parole.significato: Identical pitch between two notes or sounds; the simultaneous playing of notes of identical pitch (or separated by one…
parole.testo: From Middle English unisoun, from Middle French unisson, from Medieval Latin ūnisonus (“having the same sound”), from ūni- + sonus (“sound”).

parole.significato: the property of being universal, common to all members of a class
parole.testo: From Middle English universalite, from Middle French universalité, from Old French, from Late Latin universalitas. By surface analysis, universal + -ity.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, characteristic of, or happening or located in, a city or town; of, pertaining to, or characteristic…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French urbain (“belonging to a city, urban; courteous, refined, urbane”) (modern French urbain), or from its etymon Latin urbānus (“of or belonging to a city, urban; of manners or style: like those of city dwellers: cultivated, polished, refined, sophisticated”) + English -an (s

parole.significato: Behaviour that is polished, refined, courteous.
parole.testo: From Middle English urbanitie, from Middle French urbanité, from Latin urbānitās, from urbānus (“belonging to a city”), with a sense of "having the manners of townspeople" in Classical Latin, from urbs (“city”); equivalent to urbane + -ity (sense 1) and urban + -ity (sense 2).

parole.significato: Synonym of aurochs.
parole.testo: From Middle French ure or its etymon Latin ūrus. Doublet of urus.

parole.significato: Requiring immediate attention.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French urgent (“pressing, impelling”), from Latin urgēns, from urgēre (“to press”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ- (“bind, squeeze”). Equivalent to urge + -ent. Related to German würgen (“to strangle”), Lithuanian ver̃žti (“to string, tighten, constrict”), Russian (poetic) отв

parole.significato: Synonym of urinary.
parole.testo: From Middle French urinal, from Late Latin ūrīnālis, equivalent to urine + -al.

parole.significato: A usurper.
parole.testo: From Middle French usurpateur or Late Latin ūsūrpātor.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the uterus.
parole.testo: From Middle French utérin, from Latin uterinus (“pertaining to the womb; born of the same mother”), from Latin uterus (“womb”). Related to English uterus. By surface analysis, uter- + -ine.

parole.significato: Useful.
parole.testo: From Middle French utile, from Old French utele, from Latin ūtilis.

parole.significato: A vacation.
parole.testo: From Middle French vacance, from Medieval Latin vacantia. Doublet of vacancy.

parole.significato: Not clearly expressed; stated in indefinite terms.
parole.testo: From Middle French vague, from Latin vagus (“uncertain, vague”, literally “wandering, rambling, strolling”).

parole.significato: A man's personal male attendant, responsible for his clothes and appearance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French valet, from Old French vaslet, from Medieval Latin *vassellittus, diminutive of Late Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”) (compare Old Irish foss and

parole.significato: Well-grounded or justifiable, pertinent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French valide (“healthy, sound, in good order”), from Latin validus, from valeō (“to be strong, to be healthy, to be worth”) + -idus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“be strong”).

parole.significato: The state of being valid, authentic or genuine.
parole.testo: From valid + -ity, borrowed from Middle French validité, from Late Latin validitas.

parole.significato: The act of varying; a partial change in the form, position, state, or qualities of a thing.
parole.testo: From Middle French variation, from Old French variacion, from Latin variātiō, from vary + -ation.

parole.significato: More than one (of an indeterminate set of things).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French varieux, from Latin varius (“manifold, diverse, various, parti-colored, variegated, also changing, changeable, fickle, etc.”). By surface analysis, vary + -ous.

parole.significato: An upright open container used mainly for displaying fresh, dried, or artificial flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vase, from Latin vās. Doublet of vas.

parole.significato: Very large or wide (literally or figuratively).
parole.testo: From Middle French vaste, from Latin vastus (“void, immense”). Related to waste and German Wüste.

parole.significato: Emptiness or desolation.
parole.testo: From vast + -ity, from Middle French vastité or its source, Latin vastitas. Compare Middle English wastite.

parole.significato: Plants, taken collectively.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French végétation, from Medieval Latin vegetātiōnem.

parole.significato: Of or relating to plants; especially to their growth.
parole.testo: From Middle French végétatif, from Medieval Latin vegetativus, from past participle stem of vegetare.

parole.significato: A vector quantity that denotes the rate of change of position with respect to time, combining speed with a directional…
parole.testo: From Middle French vélocité, from Latin vēlōcitās (“speed”), from vēlōx (“fast”), thus a doublet of veloce.

parole.significato: Quality of being venomous or poisonous.
parole.testo: From Middle English venenosite, venenositee, venenoste, venenouste, from Middle French venenosite or Medieval Latin venēnōsitas. By surface analysis, venene + -osity. Piecewise doublet of venomosity.

parole.significato: Commanding respect because of age, dignity, character or position.
parole.testo: From Middle French vénérable, from Old French, from Latin venerabilis.

parole.significato: The act of venerating or the state of being venerated.
parole.testo: From Middle French vénération, from Old French veneracion, from Latin veneratio.

parole.significato: The hunting of wild animals.
parole.testo: From Middle English venerie, borrowed from Middle French venerie, from Old French venerie (“hunting”), derived from vener, from Latin vēnor (“to hunt”).

parole.significato: An opening through which gases, especially air, can pass.
parole.testo: Partly from Middle French vent, from Latin ventus and partly from French éventer. Cognate with French vent and Spanish viento (“wind”) and ventana (“window”). Doublet of wind.

parole.significato: Having a big belly.
parole.testo: From Middle French ventripotent, from Latin venter (“belly”) + potens (“powerful”).

parole.significato: The quality of speaking or stating the truth; truthfulness.
parole.testo: From Middle French véracité, from Old French veracitie, from Medieval Latin vērācitās (“truthfulness”) (whence -acity), from Latin vērāx (“truthful, speaking truth”), from vērus (“true, real”). See very.

parole.significato: The excess use of words, especially using more than are needed for clarity or precision.
parole.testo: From Middle French verbosité, from Late Latin verbōsitās. By surface analysis, verbose + -ity.

parole.significato: Green in colour.
parole.testo: From Middle French verdoyant, from Old French verb verdier, verdoier, from vert (“green”), from Vulgar Latin *virdis, from Latin viridis.

parole.significato: The greenness of lush or growing vegetation (greenery); also: the vegetation itself.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English verdure, from Middle French verdure, from Old French verdure, from Late Latin *viridūra, from viridis (“green”) + -ūra (abstract noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A rod or staff of office, e.g. of a verger.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French verge (“rod or wand of office”), hence "scope, territory dominated", from Latin virga (“shoot, rod stick”), of unknown origin. Earliest attested sense in English is now-obsolete meaning "male member, penis" (c.1400). Modern sense is from the notion of 'within the verge' (

parole.significato: The act or process of verifying.
parole.testo: From Middle French verification (modern French vérification) or its etymon Medieval Latin vērificātiō. By surface analysis, verificate + -ion.

parole.significato: The property of seeming true, of resembling reality; resemblance to reality.
parole.testo: From Middle French vérisimilitude, from Latin vērīsimilitūdō (“likeness to truth”), more correctly written separately as vērī similitūdō; from vērī, genitive singular of vērus (“true, real”), + similitūdō (“likeness, resemblance”).

parole.significato: True; genuine.
parole.testo: From verity + -able, from Middle French veritable, from Old French veritable, from Latin veritabilis.

parole.significato: A specific form or variation of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French version, from Medieval Latin versiō, from Latin vertō (“to turn”). Used in English since 16th century.

parole.significato: Standing, pointing, or moving straight up or down; parallel to the local direction of gravity; along the direction of a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vertical, from Late Latin verticālis.

parole.significato: Having an aspect of great depth, drawing the eye to look downwards.
parole.testo: From Middle French vertigineux, from Latin vertīginōsus.

parole.significato: A membrane-bound compartment found in a cell.
parole.testo: From Middle French vesicule, from Latin vēsīcula. By surface analysis, vesic- + -le. Doublet of vesicule.

parole.significato: A person with long experience of a particular activity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vétéran, from Latin veterānus.

parole.significato: Regular change or succession from one thing to another, or one part of a cycle to the next; alternation; mutual success…
parole.testo: From Middle French vicissitude, from Latin vicissitūdō (“change”), from vicissim (“on the other hand, in turn”), from vicis (“change, vicissitude”), whence Portuguese vez and French fois (“time (as in "next time"), occurrence”).

parole.significato: One that is harmed—killed, injured, subjected to oppression, deceit, or otherwise adversely affected—by someone or some…
parole.testo: From Middle French victime, from Latin victima (“sacrificial animal”). Although this root and victor drive from homophonous PIE roots, they are traditionally reconstructed as separate words and thus not cognates.

parole.significato: A person whose role it is to kill the sacrificial victim(s) during a ritual sacrifice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French victimaire, from Latin victimārius, from victima + -ārius.

parole.significato: One of a class of temporal officers who originally represented the bishops, but later were given status of fiefs, and b…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vidame, from Latin vice-dominus, from Latin vice (“instead of”) + dominus (“master, lord”).

parole.significato: Alert watchfulness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vigilance, from Latin vigilantia.

parole.significato: Vindicating, having a tendency to vindicate.
parole.testo: From Middle French vindicatif, from Medieval Latin vindicativus.

parole.significato: The act or an instance of violating or the condition of being violated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French violation, from Latin violātiō (“injury, profanation”), from violō (“to treat with violence; to maltreat; to violate, defile, profane”). Morphologically violate + -ion.

parole.significato: A venomous snake in the family Viperidae.
parole.testo: From Middle French vipere, from Old French vipre, from Latin vīpera, contracted from vīvipara f (“viviparous”, adj.), from vīvus (“alive”, adj.) + parere (“to bear”, verb). Doublet of weever and wyvern.

parole.significato: Being or resembling a virgin.
parole.testo: From Middle English virginal, from Middle French virginal, from Latin virginālis. The musical instrument is probably so called from being played by young girls.

parole.significato: A medieval punctuation mark similar to the slash ⟨/⟩ or pipe ⟨|⟩ and used as a scratch comma and caesura mark.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French virgule, from Latin virgula (“twig; scratch comma”), from virga (“rod, branch”) + -ulus (diminutive suffix). Doublet of virgula.

parole.significato: Manly; having characteristics associated with being male, such as strength; exhibiting masculine traits to an exaggerat…
parole.testo: From Middle French viril, from Latin virīlis, from vir (“man”, “male human”) + -īlis (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

parole.significato: The state of being virile.
parole.testo: From virile + -ity, from Middle French virilité, from Latin virīlitās.

parole.significato: The state of being virulent.
parole.testo: From Middle French virulence, from Late Latin virulentia.

parole.significato: The state of being viscous.
parole.testo: From Middle French viscosité, from Old French viscosité, from Medieval Latin viscositas; analysable as viscous + -ity.

parole.significato: Having a thick, sticky consistency between solid and liquid (that is, a high viscosity).
parole.testo: First attested in 1605. Borrowed from Middle French visqueux and Late Latin viscōsus, from Latin viscum (“birdlime”). Doublet of viscose.

parole.significato: A pick and hatchet in one tool for tearing down hedges.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English besagu, besague, from Middle French besague, from Old French besague, besagude, from Medieval Latin bisacūta. Doublet of besague.

parole.significato: The condition of being visible.
parole.testo: From Middle French visibilité, from Late Latin visibilitas; equivalent to visible + -ity.

parole.significato: The capacity to live and develop.
parole.testo: From vital + -ity, from Middle French vitalité, from Latin vitalitas (“vital force, life”), from vitalis (“vital”); see vital.

parole.significato: vitreous humour
parole.testo: From vitreous, from Middle French vitreux, from Latin vitreus (“glassy, transparent”), from vitrum (“glass”).

parole.significato: Of or resembling glass; glassy.
parole.testo: From Middle French vitreux, from Latin vitreus (“glassy, transparent”), from vitrum (“glass”). The terms vitreous (positive) and resinous (negative) electricity were coined in 1733 by Charles François de Cisternay du Fay, who studied the different behaviour of glass and resin when rubbed with silk a

parole.significato: To convert into glass or a glass-like substance by heat and fusion.
parole.testo: From Middle French vitrifier, from Latin vitrum (“glass”).

parole.significato: A word or utterance, especially with reference to its form rather than its meaning.
parole.testo: From Middle English vocable, from Middle French vocable and its etymon, Latin vocābulum, from vocō (“to call”).

parole.significato: The writer or maker of a vocabulary (dictionary or glossary); a lexicographer.
parole.testo: From Latin vocābulum (“vocable”) + -ist. In sense 3, probably after Middle French vocabuliste or its etymon New Latin vocābulista (“vocabulary”). With sense 1, compare French vocabuliste with the same meaning.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to calling; used in calling or vocation.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English [Term?], borrowed from Middle French vocatif, from Latin vocātīvus (“for calling”); a calque of Ancient Greek κλητῐκή (klētĭkḗ, “for calling; vocative case”) – from vocāre (“to call”), from Proto-Indo-European *wokʷ-, o-grade of *wekʷ- (“give vocal utterance, speak”). See La

parole.significato: Having extended wings as if flying.
parole.testo: From Middle French volant, present participle of voler (“to fly”), from Latin volāre.

parole.significato: Evaporating or vaporizing readily under normal conditions.
parole.testo: From Middle French volatile, from Latin volātilis (“flying; swift; temporary; volatile”), from volō (“to fly”).

parole.significato: The simultaneous firing of a number of missiles or bullets; the projectiles so fired.
parole.testo: From Middle French volée (“flight”), from Vulgar Latin volta, from Late Latin volatus.

parole.significato: Turning or whirling; winding.
parole.testo: From Middle French volubile, from Latin volūbilis (“rolling”), from volvō (“to roll”). Doublet of voluble.

parole.significato: Fluent or having a ready flow of speech.
parole.testo: From Middle French volubile, from Latin volūbilis (“rolling”), from volvō (“roll”).

parole.significato: Characterized or marked by full, generous, pleasurable sensation.
parole.testo: From Middle French voluptueux, from Latin voluptuōsus (“delightful”), from voluptās (“pleasure, delight”), from volup (“with pleasure”).

parole.significato: The state of being voracious; rapacity or extreme gluttony.
parole.testo: First attested in 1526 from Middle French voracité, from Latin vorācitās (whence -acity), from vorāx.

parole.significato: Dedicated or given in fulfillment of a vow or pledge.
parole.testo: From Middle French votif, from Latin vōtīvus (“votive”), from vōtum (“vow”).
